docs.title: Ship infrastructure changes with confidence
docs.text:
StackD is a self-hostable control plane for Terraform & OpenTofu: every change becomes a reviewable plan → human approval → apply run, executed on disposable pull-based workers, with a full audit trail and short-lived cloud credentials minted for each job. The apply runs exactly the plan that was approved.

No static cloud secrets. No shared state. No one running apply from their laptop.

docs.title: Why Stackd?
docs.text:
Running Terraform by hand doesn't scale: secrets live in CI variables, apply happens on someone's machine, the state file is a shared landmine, and "who changed prod?" has no good answer. Managed SaaS solves it — but you hand over your state, credentials, and audit log.

Stackd is the self-hosted middle ground: the API is the single source of truth, workers are stateless and disposable, every state change is one auditable event, and cloud credentials expire with the run.

docs.title: The model in one paragraph
docs.text: A space holds stacks: a stack is your code (a Git repo and a folder). Each stack is deployed as several environments (dev, prod…), each with its own state, variables and rules. Every change to an environment is a run: plan, human review, apply. A worker executes a run as jobs — a plan job, then an apply job once someone confirms. Each environment's tier decides who may confirm.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The 10-minute tour of how Stackd works inside. SPECS.md is the exhaustive technical truth; CONCEPTS.md explains each concept with worked examples.

docs.title: 🧭 System
docs.text:
The API is the single source of truth. Workers have no inbound ports — they only pull. The queue is Postgres (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), there's no broker, and Terraform talks to the API's HTTP state backend rather than to S3 directly.

flowchart LR
    Browser["SPA (React)"]
    subgraph api_box["API (FastAPI) — source of truth"]
      API["REST /api/v1 · Worker API /worker/v1<br/>state backend · OIDC issuer · WS hub · scheduler"]
    end
    PG[("PostgreSQL 18<br/>queue · audit · LISTEN/NOTIFY")]
    S3[("S3 / Garage<br/>tfstate · logs · artifacts")]
    Worker["Worker (pull agent)<br/>+ ephemeral runner"]
    Git[("Git repo")]
    STS["Cloud STS<br/>(AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity)"]

    Hooks["Slack · webhooks · GitHub"]

    Browser <-->|"REST + WebSocket"| API
    API <--> PG
    API <-->|"states · encrypted saved plans"| S3
    API -->|"ls-remote head poll · check-repo · input discovery"| Git
    API -->|"notifications · PR status/comment"| Hooks
    Worker -->|"register · heartbeat · claim · events · logs<br/>saved plan up/down (outbound only)"| API
    Worker -->|"shallow clone @ pinned commit"| Git
    Worker -->|"tofu http backend (TF_HTTP_*)"| API
    Worker -->|"OIDC token"| STS

Only the API holds the S3 and database credentials: workers reach states and saved plans through it.

docs.title: 🔄 Run state machine
docs.text:
Every state change goes through one function, transition(): it checks legality, does an atomic guarded update, writes a run_event + (for human/terminal actions) an audit_event in the same transaction, emits LISTEN/NOTIFY, and enqueues any notification. checking is skipped when there are no after_plan hooks.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> preparing: worker claims
    queued --> canceled
    queued --> discarded
    preparing --> planning
    preparing --> running: command run (import, state rm…)
    running --> finished
    running --> failed
    preparing --> failed
    planning --> checking: has after_plan hooks
    planning --> unconfirmed: diff, no autodeploy
    planning --> confirmed: autodeploy
    planning --> finished: empty diff
    checking --> unconfirmed
    checking --> confirmed
    checking --> finished
    unconfirmed --> confirmed: human confirm (can_apply + 4-eyes + mock-block)
    unconfirmed --> discarded
    unconfirmed --> canceled
    confirmed --> applying: worker claims apply (saved plan)
    applying --> finished
    planning --> failed
    checking --> failed
    applying --> failed
    finished --> [*]
    failed --> [*]
    discarded --> [*]
    canceled --> [*]

Not drawn: a closed pull request cancels its proposed runs from whatever in-flight state they are in. A user cancels only queued or unconfirmed runs: stopping a job a worker is executing is not implemented yet.

Worker loss fails only runs whose job is executing on the lost worker (preparing, planning, checking, running, applying) — after 120 s, or, for a job holding apply credentials (applying, a mutating command), after the apply budget + grace. unconfirmed and confirmed runs are never reclaimed: they wait on a human or on the apply claim. Every terminal transition drops the run's saved plan.

docs.title: 🤝 Worker pull protocol
docs.text:
One active run per environment (a partial unique index — the real concurrency guard); different environments run in parallel. What a human confirms is the plan file the plan job made: the run is pinned to the commit that plan checked out, and the apply job applies exactly that file.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Worker
    participant A as API
    participant S as S3
    participant H as Human
    W->>A: POST /worker/v1/register (pool token)
    loop every 20s
        W->>A: heartbeat → pending commands (e.g. diagnostics)
    end
    W->>A: POST /jobs/claim?wait=25 (long-poll)
    A-->>W: plan job: vars + secrets, hooks, state token (plan scope), plan OIDC token
    Note over W: clone the env branch head (or the pinned commit)
    W->>A: phase_started(planning, commit_sha)
    A->>A: pin the run to that commit
    Note over W: hooks · init · plan -out=plan.tfplan (tofu → /state/v1 via TF_HTTP_*)
    W->>A: PUT /jobs/{id}/artifacts/plan.tfplan (before after_plan hooks)
    A->>S: encrypt (AES-256-GCM) → artifacts/{run_id}/plan.tfplan
    Note over W: after_plan hooks (checking)
    W->>A: phase_finished (summary, checks) + streamed logs
    A->>A: transition() → unconfirmed
    H->>A: POST /runs/{id}/confirm
    A->>A: can_apply + 4-eyes + mock-block → confirmed
    W->>A: claim (the plan's worker first for 60 s, then any compatible worker)
    A-->>W: apply job: pinned commit, state token (rw scope), apply OIDC token, apply budget
    Note over W: clone the pinned commit · init
    W->>A: GET /jobs/{id}/artifacts/plan.tfplan
    A->>S: fetch + decrypt
    A-->>W: plan.tfplan (missing or unreadable → the job fails closed, no re-plan)
    Note over W: before_apply · apply plan.tfplan · output -json · after_apply
    W->>A: phase_finished (outputs, apply-stage checks)
    A->>A: transition() → finished (saved plan deleted), then cascade downstream

Per-job state tokens. Each claim mints a state token for that job only, with a scope fixed at mint time: ro (a PR or drift plan, a read-only command: read only, no lock), plan (a plan job: read and lock while planning, never write), rw (an apply or a mutating command: write; TTL = the apply budget + grace). A token whose run has ended can no longer write or lock. The worker hands it to tofu only, as TF_HTTP_* environment variables — hooks never see it.

Hooks and checks. Platform hooks run first, then the repo's .stackd.yml hooks; a repo hook gets no secret (an allowlisted env, a masked plan.json, no tfvars or token file on disk). Every check result, with the stage it ran at, is kept on the run (check_results). A failing fail check stops the job at its stage; a failing after_apply check fails the run after the infrastructure changed: its outputs are recorded, nothing cascades.

Apply affinity. A confirmed run is reserved for the worker that planned it for 60 s, then any compatible worker takes it. Nothing is carried over in the workspace: the apply always starts from a fresh clone of the pinned commit and the saved plan from the API.

docs.title: 🧬 Dependencies, mocks & cascade
docs.text:
At claim the API resolves each referenced input as real upstream output › mock › explicit error. A run that consumed a mock is flagged used_mocks and can't be applied unless the env opts in. When a tracked apply finishes, downstream environments cascade — protections are never bypassed.

flowchart TD
    subgraph net["network/prod (upstream)"]
      NO["output: network_name"]
    end
    subgraph app["app/prod (downstream)"]
      direction TB
      R{"resolve input<br/>network_name"}
      R -->|"real output exists"| Real["use real value"]
      R -->|"no output, mock set"| Mock["use mock → used_mocks=true<br/>apply blocked (allow_mock_apply=false)"]
      R -->|"no output, no mock"| Err["run fails: missing_upstream_output"]
    end
    NO -.->|"captured on apply"| R
    NetApply["network/prod apply finishes"] -->|"cascade (tracked)"| AppRun["new app/prod run"]
    AppRun --> R

docs.title: 🔔 Notifications — transactional outbox
docs.text:
transition() enqueues a row in notification_outbox in the same transaction (no I/O in the request path). The scheduler drains it under an advisory lock with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so a rolled-back transition never notifies and two API replicas never double-send. No DB transaction is held during the HTTP call.

flowchart LR
    T["transition() → unconfirmed / finished / failed"] -->|"same txn"| OB[("notification_outbox")]
    SCH["scheduler tick<br/>(advisory lock + SKIP LOCKED)"] -->|"drain unsent"| OB
    SCH -->|"match stack/env targets on_states"| DNS["resolve host once<br/>every IP must be public"]
    DNS -->|"https POST to the vetted IP<br/>(no env proxy, no redirect)"| POST["Slack / webhook"]
    POST -->|"ok → sent_at"| OB
    POST -->|"fail → retry (≤5)"| OB

The POST dials the address the SSRF check vetted, with Host, SNI and certificate checks on the original hostname, so DNS rebinding can't redirect it to an internal host. It deliberately ignores HTTPS_PROXY and other env proxies (a proxy would resolve the name again): an API whose only egress is a proxy cannot deliver notifications. The PR status/comment post-back (vcs_outbox) follows the same outbox pattern.

docs.title: 🗂️ Variable resolution
docs.text:
Variables resolve in layers, with provenance — the most specific layer wins, and the UI shows where each value came from. Only variable sets of the environment's own space apply:

flowchart LR
    S1["sets by rule<br/>(auto_attach · label selector)"] --> R
    S0["tier-attached sets"] --> R
    S2["stack-attached sets"] --> R
    S3["env-attached sets"] --> R
    ST["stack variables"] --> R
    EN["env variables"] --> R
    R{{"resolve<br/>(most specific wins)"}} --> OUT["value + provenance badge"]

Upstream outputs and mocks (dependency:, mock) and external secret references are merged in at claim time.

docs.title: 📈 Scaling
docs.text:
Workers are stateless pull agents, so scaling out = running more of them (e.g. bumping an ECS service desiredCount). Postgres serializes claims with two guards (FOR UPDATE … SKIP LOCKED + the one_active_run_per_env unique index). What's worth knowing:

  • 🧩 The unit of parallelism is the environment, not the worker — one active run per env, but different envs run concurrently. Throughput ≈ min(workers, envs with queued work).
  • 🏷️ Labels segment pools — a worker only claims runs whose env labels are a subset of its own, so you can dedicate (and scale) a prod pool independently.
  • ♻️ Workers are interchangeable & disposable — apply affinity prefers the worker that planned for 60 s, but the apply never depends on it (pinned commit + saved plan from the API). Losing a worker only fails the runs executing on it (worker_lost); runs waiting for a human or for the apply claim survive.
  • 🔁 Each worker runs STACKD_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS jobs at once (default 1), always on different environments.
  • 🗓️ The scheduler runs in every API replica, each task under its own advisory lock (held on a dedicated connection), so a task runs once per tick across replicas. The git head poll runs as a separate task (at most 8 ls-remote at a time), so slow repos never delay worker-loss detection or notifications.
  • 📊 No built-in autoscaler, but /api/v1/health and /queue expose the signals an external one (ECS target-tracking, KEDA) can drive; /metrics serves Prometheus gauges. On Fargate, mind the runner execution model (no DinD).

docs.title: CONCEPTS.md — Stackd concepts, explained with examples
docs.text: A concept guide for everyone using or building Stackd. It teaches the mental model with concrete, copy-pasteable examples. For the exhaustive field-by-field truth, see SPECS.md — this document never contradicts it, it illustrates it.

docs.title: Key concepts at a glance
docs.text:
Read this first if you are new to Stackd: each line is expanded, with examples, in the numbered section given in the last column.

Space                  a team or project boundary: who can see and do what
└── Stack              the code: a Git repo + a folder (the template)
    ├── Environment    dev      ┐ real deployments of that code, each with its own
    ├── Environment    staging  ├ state, variables and rules
    └── Environment    prod     ┘
        └── Run        one change to one environment: plan → review → apply
            ├── Job    plan job: a worker plans the change and runs the checks
            └── Job    apply job: a worker applies the reviewed plan
Concept What it is Why it matters § Space A boundary for a team or project, holding its stacks, variable sets and worker pools. Members get a role and a set of tiers per space; nothing crosses from one space to another. 1 Stack The code: a Git repository, a folder in it, and the tool (OpenTofu or Terraform). Written once, deployed many times. A stack never runs on its own. 2 Environment One real deployment of a stack (dev, prod…): its branch, state, variables and protections. Environments are fully isolated from each other — the opposite of Terraform workspaces. 2 Variables & variable sets The code's inputs, set on the environment, the stack, or in sets shared across stacks. The most specific value wins and the UI shows where each value came from. Secrets are write-only. 3 Run One change to one environment: plan, wait for review, apply exactly the reviewed plan. It is the unit of change, of review and of audit. One active run per environment at a time. 4 Job One piece of a run that a worker executes: the plan job, then — once confirmed — the apply job. A command run has a single command job. The two jobs of a run can land on different workers: the apply job starts from a fresh clone and the saved plan. 4 Tier A label on an environment (dev, prod, or your own). Decides who may approve it, and whether someone other than the person who started the run must confirm. 5 Role reader (looks), writer (starts runs, edits configuration), approver (also confirms applies on their tiers), admin (also manages workers, users and settings). Approving needs both the role and the environment's tier in your allowed tiers. 5 Hook A command run at a fixed step of a job: a security scan, a cost check, a policy. Platform hooks are enforced and trusted; hooks from the repo run without secrets. Each result is kept on the run as a check. 6 Worker The agent that runs OpenTofu on your infrastructure. It pulls its jobs (no inbound port), keeps nothing between jobs and can be replaced at any time. 7 Managed state The tfstate, stored by Stackd in S3 behind its own HTTP backend. Each job gets a short-lived token scoped to what it may do: read (a pull request's plan), lock (a plan), or write (an apply). 8 Dependency & mock One environment's outputs feeding another's inputs (network → app). An upstream change re-plans its dependents. A mock lets a new chain plan before its upstream exists, but blocks the apply by default. 9 Cloud credentials (OIDC) Short-lived cloud credentials minted for each job. No static cloud keys to store or rotate; the plan job assumes the plan role (read-only), the apply job the apply role. 10 Staleness "This environment is behind its branch." Tells you a merged change hasn't been applied yet; it never triggers anything by itself. 11 Audit An append-only record of every action, written with the action itself. Answers "who changed prod, and why?" 12

docs.title: The life of a change
docs.text:
1. Someone pushes, opens a pull request, or clicks Plan. Stackd creates a run for the environment(s) tracking that branch. A pull request only ever gets a read-only plan.
  2. A worker runs the plan job: it checks out the exact commit and plans with credentials minted for this job only. Hooks check the plan.
  3. The run waits for a human (unless the environment autodeploys a clean plan). An approver allowed on that tier reads the diff, the checks and every input with its origin, then confirms or discards. If the tier or the environment requires four-eyes, that approver can't be the person who started the run.
  4. A worker runs the apply job: it applies the saved plan — exactly what was reviewed, on the same commit.
  5. If the outputs changed, dependent environments re-plan under their own approval rules. Everything above is in the audit log.

docs.title: Following the examples
docs.text:
All examples assume the local dev stack is up (task dev) with the API on http://localhost:8000 and dev login enabled. Authenticate once:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/auth/dev/login \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"persona":"admin"}' | jq -r .access_token)
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: 0. The one-sentence mental model
docs.text:
Stackd orchestrates plan → human confirmation → apply of Terraform/OpenTofu on pull-based workers, where the API is the single source of truth and every state change is an auditable event.

Everything below is a refinement of that sentence.

docs.title: 1. Space — the container
docs.text:
A space is the top of the hierarchy: space / stack / environment / run. It owns stacks, variable sets, worker pools and secret sources. The bootstrap creates default (the dev seed adds demo), and an instance admin can create more. A space is also a permission boundary: each member has a membership in it (role, allowed tiers, destroy right), you only see and touch the spaces you belong to (an instance admin reaches all), and configuration never crosses spaces (§3).

default                      ← space
└── core-network             ← stack   (a repo + a folder)
    ├── dev                  ← environment (an instance with its own state)
    ├── staging
    └── prod

docs.title: 2. Stack vs Environment — template vs instance
docs.text:
This is the most important distinction in Stackd.

Stack Environment What it is a template: a Git repo + a subfolder + which tool an instance: one real deployment Holds repo_url, project_root, tool, tool_version tier, branch, state, variables, protections Analogy a class an object Runs? never a run always belongs to an environment

Why not Terraform workspaces? Workspaces share code, backend and credentials and only suffix the state key — easy to target the wrong one. A Stackd environment is physically isolated: its own state, variables, protections and worker pool.

Example — one stack, three environments:

# Stack = the template
STACK=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks -H "$AUTH" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"core-network","repo_url":"https://github.com/acme/infra",
       "project_root":"network","tool":"opentofu","tool_version":"1.12.0"}' | jq -r .id)

# Environments = instances of that template
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/environments -H "$AUTH" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"dev","tier":"dev","branch":"main"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/environments -H "$AUTH" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"prod","tier":"prod","branch":"main","protected":true,"require_second_pair_of_eyes":true}'

dev and prod run the same code but have different state, variables, tier and protections.

docs.title: 3. Variables & variable sets — configuration in layers
docs.text:
Configuration is composed from layers. The same variable name can be defined at several layers; the strongest layer wins. From weakest to strongest:

1. variable sets applying by rule          (auto_attach, or a label selector matching
                                            the environment)
2. variable sets attached to a tier        (by priority)
3. variable sets attached to a stack       (by priority)
4. variable sets attached to an environment (by priority)
5. stack variables                         (common to all environments of the stack)
6. environment variables                   ← always wins

A variable set is a named, reusable bundle (e.g. common-aws, datadog, region-eu) you attach to many stacks and environments. auto_attach: true means "attach to every stack in the space"; a selector ({label: value}) attaches it to every environment whose labels match.

A set stays in its space. You can only attach it to a stack or environment of the set's own space (400 Cross-space attachment otherwise), and a tier attachment reaches that tier's environments in the set's space only — tiers are a global catalog, the set is not. Deleting a stack or an environment removes the attachments that target it.

Worked example. Suppose:

Layer defines set common-aws (auto_attach) region = eu-west-1, tags = {team:core} set region-us (attached to environment prod-us) region = us-east-1 stack variable cidr = 10.0.0.0/16 environment variable on prod-us cidr = 10.9.0.0/16

Resolving variables for prod-us:

Variable Value Provenance region us-east-1 set:region-us (a set attached to the environment beats auto_attach) tags {team:core} set:common-aws cidr 10.9.0.0/16 env (the environment's override beats the stack variable)

See it for real:

curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV/resolved-variables -H "$AUTH" | jq
# [{ "name":"region","injected_name":"TF_VAR_region","value":"us-east-1","provenance":"set:region-us" }, ...]

Every resolved variable carries its provenance so the UI can show "inherited from common-aws" or "overridden here". The provenance is also frozen onto the run (variable_provenance) for audit.

docs.title: Variable kinds
docs.text:
• terraform → written to an auto-loaded tfvars file that exists only while tofu runs (listed as TF_VAR_<name>).
  • environment → injected as a process environment variable for the run.

docs.title: Sensitive variables are write-only
docs.text:
Mark a variable sensitive: true and it is AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest and never returned in clear — the API masks it as •••, decrypting only to build the worker payload, and the agent masks the literal value in logs.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/variables -H "$AUTH" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"kind":"environment","name":"DD_API_KEY","value":"super-secret","sensitive":true}'
# GET later → "value":"•••"   (the plaintext is never readable again through the API)

docs.title: 4. Runs & the state machine
docs.text:
A run is one change to one environment, from plan to apply. Its life is an explicit state machine — and the only way the state ever changes is the transition() function, which writes a run_event, an audit_event (for human/terminal actions) and a live WebSocket signal, all in one DB transaction.

queued → preparing → planning → [checking] → unconfirmed → confirmed → applying → finished
                                                  │ discard → discarded
   (terminal: finished · failed · discarded · canceled)
  • checking only appears if there are after_plan hooks.
  • unconfirmed = waiting for a human (the amber state — see DESIGN).
  • If the plan has no changes, the run jumps straight to finished.

Run and job. A run is the change; a job is what a worker executes for it. A run that goes all the way has two jobs: the plan job (preparing → planning → checking: clone, hooks, init, plan, checks) and, once confirmed, the apply job (applying: fresh clone, apply the saved plan, outputs). They can run on different workers. A command run (import, state rm…) has one command job; a pull request's run has only a plan job. Hooks, credentials and state tokens are per job.

Example — a manual plan that needs confirmation:

# 1. trigger → run is created 'queued'
RUN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV/runs -H "$AUTH" -d '{}' | jq -r .id)

# 2. a worker claims it → preparing → planning, then reports a non-empty plan → 'unconfirmed'
# 3. a human confirms (subject to permissions, §5)
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/runs/$RUN/confirm -H "$AUTH"
# → confirmed → a worker claims the apply → applying → finished

What gets applied is exactly what was reviewed. The plan job saves its plan.tfplan; the API encrypts it and keeps it in S3 until the run ends. The run is pinned to the commit the plan checked out, and the apply job clones that commit and runs tofu apply plan.tfplan — it never re-plans. If the saved plan is missing, or the state moved since the plan (tofu refuses a stale plan), the run fails: trigger a new plan.

Concurrency invariant: at most one active run per environment (enforced by a partial unique index). Two environments of the same stack can run in parallel; two runs on the same environment cannot.

docs.title: 5. Tiers, roles & permissions — who can apply what
docs.text:
Two orthogonal axes:

  • role (global capability): reader < writer < approver < admin. What you can do in nature (read, manage config, confirm, administer).
  • tier on the environment (a configurable catalog, e.g. dev/staging/prod/qa) × allowed_tiers set on the user. Where you can apply.

Anyone (writer+) can trigger a plan on any environment — a plan changes nothing. Only the apply confirmation is gated.

can_apply(user, env) = role ∈ {approver, admin} AND env.tier ∈ user.allowed_tiers (set membership — tiers are not ordered, so a grant can be non-contiguous like {dev, prod}).

Examples:

User role allowed tiers dev staging prod Bob writer {dev, staging} ❌ (not approver) ❌ ❌ Carol approver {dev, staging} ✅ ✅ ❌ (prod not in her set) Alice approver {dev, staging, prod} ✅ ✅ ✅ Dan approver {dev, prod} ✅ ❌ ✅

These are the effective permissions in the environment's space: a space membership can give someone a different role, tier set or destroy right there than their instance defaults.

Extra rules:

  • Destroy (type=destroy) additionally requires can_destroy=true — a separate, explicit right.
  • Four-eyes: on a tier flagged requires_four_eyes (the seeded prod), on a protected environment, or when the environment sets require_second_pair_of_eyes, someone other than the person who triggered the run must confirm it. It only bites human-triggered runs — a webhook or cascade run has no human to oppose.
  • Mock block: a run that consumed mock outputs cannot be applied unless allow_mock_apply=true (see §9).

When a confirm is refused, the API returns the reason in clear, e.g. 403 "tier prod not in your allowed tiers (dev, staging)", which the UI shows on the disabled Confirm button.

Double lock with the cloud: for prod, the restriction also lives in the AWS trust policy (§10), so bypassing the API still can't assume the prod apply role.

docs.title: 6. Hooks & checks — custom flow steps
docs.text:
Hooks run shell commands at lifecycle stages: before_init, after_init, before_plan, after_plan, before_apply, after_apply. They come from two sources, merged:

Source Where Editable by Use Platform UI/API (per stack or environment) writer+ (audited) governance — not bypassable by a PR Repo .stackd.yml in the repo anyone who pushes project-specific logic

Order per stage: platform (stack) → platform (environment) → repo. Security-critical checks belong on the platform side. The plan job runs the *_init, *_plan stages; the apply job the *_apply ones.

.stackd.yml example:

version: 1
hooks:
  after_plan:
    - name: infracost
      command: infracost breakdown --path plan.json --format table
      on_failure: warn          # run continues but MUST be confirmed by a human
    - name: no-prod-deletes
      command: jq -e '[.resource_changes[]|select(.change.actions|index("delete"))]|length==0' plan.json
      on_failure: fail          # run → failed
  • on_failure: fail → the job stops at that stage and the run fails (run.check_failed), at every stage. A failing before_apply hook means nothing is applied. A failing after_apply hook fails the run after the infrastructure changed: its outputs are still recorded, but nothing cascades.
  • on_failure: warn → the run continues but is forced through unconfirmed even if autodeploy was on — a human must own the warning. (At an apply stage the run is already confirmed: the warning is only recorded.)
  • Each hook has 10 minutes (STACKD_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS on the worker); past it, it is killed and fails by its on_failure. If tofu can't produce the plan JSON, the plan job fails rather than check an empty plan.

Checks. Every hook result is a check, kept on the run with the stage it ran at (check_results.results: ok, warn, fail; check_results.checks: only warn/fail).

Repo hooks get nothing secret: of the worker's environment only an allowlist (PATH, HOME, locale, proxies…), the run's non-sensitive environment variables, no cloud credentials, and a plan.json with every sensitive value masked. While a repo hook runs, neither the saved plan, the run's tfvars, the cloud token file nor the repo token is on disk. Platform hooks are trusted: they get the run's secrets, the cloud credentials and the raw plan.json. Neither tofu nor any hook sees the agent's own STACKD_* settings. See Hooks.

docs.title: 7. Workers — the pull model
docs.text:
Workers are self-hosted, stateless and disposable. They pull work; the API never connects out to them.

register (pool token) → heartbeat (every ~20s) → claim (long-poll)
   → clone → hooks → init → plan/apply → stream logs → report → repeat
  • Claim is concurrency-safe: SELECT … FOR UPDATE OF environment SKIP LOCKED serialises per environment, and the one_active_run_per_env unique index is the hard guarantee (a losing racer gets a 23505 and simply re-polls).
  • Labels target work to pools (e.g. a dedicated prod pool).
  • Apply affinity: the worker that produced a plan is preferred for the apply for ~60s; past that, any compatible worker takes it. Either way the apply worker starts from a fresh clone of the pinned commit and applies the saved plan it downloads from the API (§4) — no workspace is reused, nothing is re-planned.
  • Per-job credentials: each job gets its own state token, scoped to what it does — ro for a PR plan or a read-only command, plan for a plan job (it may lock, never write), rw for an apply job or a mutating command (§8) — and its own cloud credentials: the plan role for a plan job, the apply role for an apply job (§10).
  • Worker loss: a worker silent > 60s → offline. A run whose job is executing on it (preparing, planning, checking, running, applying) → failed (worker_lost) after 120s. A job holding apply credentials (an applying run, a mutating command) is only reclaimed after the apply budget + grace (15 + 5 min by default), so a long apply isn't failed mid-flight and its tokens have expired before another worker takes the environment. unconfirmed and confirmed runs are never reclaimed: they wait on a human or on the apply claim, not on the plan worker.
  • Command channel. The heartbeat response is also the downward channel (still no inbound to the worker). Today it carries diagnostics: an admin clicks a button, a pending command is queued, the worker picks it up on its next heartbeat, runs a read-only bundle (versions, disk, environment variable names — never values, recent agent logs) and posts it back. Same mechanism will carry cancel_job later. Delivery latency is bounded by the heartbeat interval (~20 s).

Run an agent:

POOL=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/worker-pools -H "$AUTH" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"local"}' | jq -r .token)
cd worker && STACKD_POOL_TOKEN=$POOL STACKD_API_URL=http://localhost:8000 uv run python -m agent.main

docs.title: 8. Managed state — S3 behind an HTTP backend
docs.text:
The tfstate bytes live in S3, but Terraform talks to Stackd's HTTP backend, not S3 directly.

terraform ──backend "http"──▶ Stackd API ──(SSE-KMS)──▶ S3
                                  └─▶ Postgres: versions, locks, audit

Why: per-job scoped tokens, locking visible in the UI with audited force-unlock, refusal of a regressive serial, and every write tied to the run that produced it. The token's scope follows the job: ro (PR plans, read-only commands: read only), plan (a plan may lock, never write), rw (an apply or a mutating command). Once its run has ended, a token can no longer write or lock.

The worker adds a bare backend "http" {} block and hands the address and the token to tofu only, as TF_HTTP_* environment variables — never -backend-config, which tofu would persist in .terraform/ (readable by repo hooks) and in the saved plan. Zero changes to the user's Terraform code: the repo declares no backend. Set managed_state: false to keep your own backend "s3".

docs.title: 9. Dependencies, outputs & mocks — the differentiator
docs.text:
Environments can depend on each other and pass outputs as inputs. Example: app/dev needs the network_name produced by network/dev.

# app/dev depends on network/dev: map upstream output → downstream input, with a mock for bootstrap
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$APP_DEV/dependencies -H "$AUTH" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "upstream_env_id":"'$NET_DEV'",
  "trigger_policy":"on_output_change",
  "references":[{"output_name":"network_name","input_name":"network_name","mock_value":"mock-network"}]
}'

Resolution rule at claim time: real value > mock > explicit error.

Situation What app/dev gets network/dev already applied, output exists the real value, provenance dependency:core-network/dev network/dev never applied, a mock_value exists the mock, run flagged used_mocks=true network/dev never applied, no mock run fails immediately (missing_upstream_output) upstream output is sensitive config error (sensitive outputs are never propagated)

Mocks solve the chicken-and-egg of bootstrapping a cascade: you can plan app/dev with network_name = "mock-network" before network/dev has ever run — to validate config. But a run that used mocks cannot be applied (allow_mock_apply=false by default) — a mocked plan is for validation, not for real changes. The UI shows a violet MOCKED badge.

Cascade. When network/dev finishes an apply, Stackd captures its outputs and triggers the downstream app/dev run automatically (triggered_by=dependency), passing the now-real value. The cascade never bypasses protections — a protected downstream still stops at unconfirmed.

network/dev  ──apply finished──▶  capture outputs  ──cascade──▶  app/dev run (real network_name)

docs.title: 10. OIDC workload credentials — zero static cloud secrets
docs.text:
Stackd is itself an OIDC issuer. At each claim it signs a short-lived workload token scoped to the run and phase; AWS exchanges it for a role via AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. No static AWS keys anywhere.

Token subject (the basis of trust policies):

sub = run:<tier>:<stack>:<phase>      e.g.  run:prod:core-network:apply

Plan and apply assume different roles — a PR plan physically cannot modify infra:

# Trust policy of the prod APPLY role — refuses everything else
condition {
  test     = "StringLike"
  variable = "stackd.example.com:sub"
  values   = ["run:prod:*:apply"]   # any stack, but tier=prod AND phase=apply
}

The wildcard is allowed only on the stack segment — tier and phase are always fixed; that's the double lock with §5. The worker exports AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE / AWS_ROLE_ARN to tofu and platform hooks only — never to repo hooks — and the token file exists only while one of them runs. The AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME = stackd-<run_id> ties every CloudTrail action back to the run — and thus to the human who confirmed it.

curl -s -X PUT localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$PROD/cloud-integration -H "$AUTH" -d '{
  "plan_role_arn":"arn:aws:iam::123:role/stackd-prod-plan",
  "apply_role_arn":"arn:aws:iam::123:role/stackd-prod-apply","region":"eu-west-1"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$PROD/cloud-integration/test -H "$AUTH"  # verify AssumeRole

docs.title: 11. Webhooks & Git staleness
docs.text:
A Git webhook (HMAC-verified, secret per repo) maps a pushed branch to the environments tracking it, filtered by project_root:

  • push → a tracked run per matching environment, and head_sha advances.
  • pull request → a proposed run: plan-only, read-only state, mocks allowed, and no secrets: the pull request's code runs inside tofu, so it gets none of the environment's sensitive variables — only the read-only plan role — see Runs & approvals.

Staleness answers "applied ≠ tip of branch": Stackd compares the commit of the last finished tracked run (every run is pinned to the commit it planned) to the branch head (head_sha, refreshed by webhook, by git ls-remote polling every 15 min, or manually). The API exposes it on each environment (stale, commits_ahead); the ↑N chip and the Re-plan banner on a stale unconfirmed run (DESIGN §5.1–5.2) are not in the UI yet. Changing an environment's branch resets its recorded head; a push deleting the branch clears it. Staleness is information, never an automatic trigger.

docs.title: 12. Audit vs logs — two different journals
docs.text:
Audit (audit_events) Logs (structured JSON) Question who did what, when what is the system doing / why is it broken Examples run.confirmed, run.applied, user.role_changed run.transition, worker.claim, http.request Storage Postgres, append-only at the DB level (INSERT-only role + trigger), 2 years in-memory ring buffer + stdout, ephemeral Written in the same transaction as the action best-effort, never blocks the request Audience compliance, "who applied to prod last week?" operators debugging

They never duplicate each other: a login is an audit event, not a debug log.

curl -s "localhost:8000/api/v1/audit?action=run.applied" -H "$AUTH" | jq   # who applied what

docs.title: 13. Observability — health & logs at a glance
docs.text:
• GET /api/v1/health — DB check, workers (online/total + last heartbeat), runs (active/queued), recent warnings/errors. The front Workers & health page renders this with a live logs panel, and a green/red dot sits in the topbar.
  • GET /api/v1/logs (admin) — the structured JSON ring buffer, filterable by level, event, worker_id, run_id, request_id, free-text q. Every HTTP response carries an X-Request-ID so you can correlate a request across all its log lines.

Log levels carry signal, not volume: mutations and domain events (run.transition, worker.claim, …) are INFO; reads, polls and heartbeats are DEBUG (hidden by default); all 4xx are WARNING, 5xx are ERROR. Set STACKD_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG to see everything.

  • Worker diagnostics: from the Workers page, a per-worker button runs the read-only bundle (§7) — the simplest remote debug without opening a shell.
  • First-login walkthrough: a short tour explains the model on first connection. "Seen" is stored server-side (users.onboarded_at) — never in browser storage (invariant #8).

docs.title: 14. Notifications — closing the human-in-the-loop
docs.text:
The product's heart is plan → human confirmation → apply. Notifications make sure the human actually learns a decision is waiting — without staring at the UI.

A notification target is an outbound webhook attached to a stack or an environment (exactly like a platform hook), firing on a chosen set of run states:

state when it fires typical use unconfirmed a plan is ready and awaits confirmation ping the approver: "prod apply waiting" failed a run failed alert on breakage finished a run finished (incl. apply) deploy log / changelog

Two kinds: slack (posts {"text": …} to a Slack/Mattermost incoming webhook, with a deep link to the run) and webhook (a structured JSON envelope: state, run id, stack/environment, tier, commit, url).

Example — Slack the approver whenever a prod apply is pending:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV_ID/notifications -H "$AUTH" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
    "name": "prod-approvals",
    "kind": "slack",
    "url": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ",
    "on_states": ["unconfirmed", "failed"]
  }'

How it works — a transactional outbox, not a side-effect. When transition() moves a run to a notify-worthy state, it inserts a row into notification_outbox in the same DB transaction as the state change (no HTTP in the request path). A background scheduler task drains the outbox under a pg_try_advisory_lock (one replica at a time) with FOR UPDATE … SKIP LOCKED, resolves the matching targets (those on the run's environment + those on its stack, filtered by on_states), and POSTs — with no DB transaction held during the HTTP call. Consequences worth knowing:

  • a rolled-back transition never notifies (the outbox row rolls back with it);
  • two API replicas never double-send (the lock + SKIP LOCKED);
  • delivery is at-least-once with retries (up to 5 attempts), then the row is dead-lettered and the failure is logged — a flaky Slack never blocks or fails a run.

Deep links use STACKD_APP_URL (the SPA base, e.g. http://localhost:5173).

SSRF guard. A target URL must be https and its host must resolve to public addresses only (no private, loopback, link-local or metadata IP), checked at create/update and again at every delivery. The POST connects to the IP that check vetted (Host, SNI and certificate stay on the hostname), never follows redirects, and ignores HTTPS_PROXY and other proxy variables by design: a proxy would resolve the name again. An API whose only egress is a proxy cannot deliver notifications. Targets are deleted with their stack or environment.

docs.title: 15. Quick reference
docs.text: Term One line Space top container and permission boundary (default, plus any an admin creates) Stack template: repo + folder + tool Environment instance: tier + branch + state + variables + protections Variable set reusable bundle of variables, attached to tiers, stacks or environments of its own space Provenance where a resolved variable came from (set:…, stack, env, dependency:…, mock) Run one change to one environment, from plan to apply, driven by the state machine Job what a worker executes for a run: the plan job, the apply job, or a command job transition() the only thing that changes a run's state Tier configurable catalog; gates apply via the user's allowed_tiers set (not ordered) Four-eyes the person who triggered a run can't confirm it, on a requires_four_eyes tier, a protected environment, or when the environment requires it Hook shell step at a lifecycle stage; platform (governance, trusted) or repo (no secrets) Check a hook's result (ok, warn, fail), kept on the run with its stage Worker stateless agent that pulls and runs jobs Managed state tfstate in S3 via Stackd's HTTP backend, per-job scoped tokens Saved plan the reviewed plan.tfplan, kept encrypted until the run ends; the apply applies exactly it Mock output placeholder value to bootstrap a cascade; blocks the apply unless the environment sets allow_mock_apply Cascade downstream runs triggered when an upstream apply finishes Workload token per-job OIDC token, sub=run:<tier>:<stack>:<phase> Audit who-did-what, append-only Proposed run plan-only run from a PR (ro state token, plan role, no secrets) Notification target outbound Slack/webhook on a stack or environment, firing on chosen run states Outbox run-event notifications enqueued in-txn, drained by the scheduler (at-least-once)

docs.title: DESIGN.md — Front-end design decisions
docs.text: Companion to PLAN.md and SPECS.md. This document locks in the design decisions for the interface: visual direction, tokens, navigation, patterns for the key screens. Goal: that every screen built (by a human or by Claude Code) is consistent without re-litigating the choices.

docs.title: 1. Subject, audience, intent
docs.text:
• Subject: a control room for infrastructure. You come here to quickly answer three questions: what is running?, what is waiting on a human decision?, who did what?
  • Audience: cloud/DevOps/SRE engineers. Expert, daily users, on the keyboard, often on a large screen, sometimes on call on whatever screen is at hand. Zero need for marketing seduction in the app.
  • Emotional intent: operational confidence. The interface of a tool that applies destructive changes to production must be calm, dense, legible, unambiguous. No gamification, no decoration, no gratuitous animation.
  • Anti-references: the "generic SaaS dashboard" look (floating rounded cards, gradients, 3D illustrations) and the "hacker terminal" look (pure black + acid green). Both are defaults, not choices.

docs.title: 2.1 Concept: "operational blueprint"
docs.text:
The aesthetic draws on technical drawings and engineering schematics: deep slate-blue backgrounds, fine strokes, monospace labels, hierarchy carried by typography and rules rather than by shadowed boxes. It is the natural universe of the subject (you draw infrastructure) and it ages well.

  • Dark-first: the dark theme is the reference theme (logs, on-call duty, the habits of the trade). A light theme exists from the start (same token system, never "added later").
  • Deliberately high density: compact tables, tight line-height on data, generous margins only around decision areas. Density is a service rendered to an expert, not a defect.
  • Flat and delimited by rules: separations via 1px borders and subtle background variations. No drop shadows, no glassmorphism. Low radius (4 px) — the tool is angular like a schematic.

docs.title: 2.2 Signature element: the phase rail
docs.text:
THE memorable thing about the interface: a vertical rail present on every run page, which materializes the state machine (queued → preparing → planning → checking → unconfirmed → applying → finished; checking only appears if the plan ran after_plan hooks, confirmed is transient and is displayed as the start of the applying segment). Each segment:

  • semantic color code (cf. §3.2), the active segment animated with a discreet pulse (the only ambient animation in the app);
  • clickable: navigates directly to the log section for that phase;
  • carries its metadata in mono (duration, exit code, number of checks);
  • reused as a horizontal miniature everywhere a run is listed (stacks table, audit, run groups) — a visual signature you learn once and re-read everywhere.

The rail IS the product's pedagogy: it makes the state machine visible instead of explaining it.

docs.title: 3.1 Palette (dark theme, reference)
docs.text:
Token Hex Usage bg-base #0C1118 app background (bluish slate, never pure black) bg-surface #141B24 panels, tables bg-raised #1D2733 interactive elements, hover, sticky headers border #2A3542 1px rules (the main structural material) text-primary #E8EEF4 body text text-secondary #8A97A4 labels, meta accent #8B6CF0 (brand violet) structure: focus, active links/nav, primary CTAs, the mark decision #E8A838 (signal amber) the human-decision moment only: Confirm / apply

Two accents, two jobs. The brand violet (from the StackD logo) is the structural accent — focus rings, active nav, links, primary CTAs, the wordmark's "D". Amber means "needs a human" and nothing else: the Confirm/apply decision, the unconfirmed state, and review signals that ask for human judgment — warn checks/hooks, open discussion threads, a secret resolved via fallback. Keeping it narrow means amber stands out from the violet chrome — the most important button in the app is amber, not green ("your judgment is needed", not "all is well"). Amber is not used for technical telemetry (log severity, HTTP status, latency) — that surface only reddens genuine failures and stays neutral otherwise. Two established conventions are separate: the plan diff's ~ modified (green/amber/red) and ANSI yellow in logs. The green/red spectrum stays free for state semantics.

Light theme: same tokens (bg-base #F7F9FB, navy #1B2733 for text — the logo's own colour, brand violet #6D3FD4 and darkened amber #A87A1F for AA contrast).

docs.title: 3.2 State colors (the semantic language, identical in both themes)
docs.text:
State Color Hex (dark) Where queued / neutral gray #6E7B8B badges, rail, graph nodes running (preparing/planning/checking/applying) blue #4C8DFF + pulse on the active element unconfirmed (waiting on a human) amber #E8A838 the same color as decision: waiting on a human IS the action finished green #3FB950 failed red #F85149 discarded / canceled struck-through gray #6E7B8B

mocked is not a state but a modifier that overlays the current state (a mocked run is also unconfirmed, planning...) — rendered by a distinct magenta badge #EC6AB4, deliberately outside the operational spectrum ("this is not real"): MOCKED badge, mocked values. (Magenta, not purple — purple is now the brand.)

Absolute rule: these colors serve only state semantics. Never decorative blue, never green on a button unrelated to a success. This is what makes the app legible at a glance at 3 a.m.

docs.title: 3.3 Typography
docs.text:
Role Font Usage UI / body IBM Plex Sans navigation, forms, prose Data / structure JetBrains Mono ⭐ everything that is data: IDs, SHAs, resource names, variable values, durations, eyebrow labels, column headers, logs Display IBM Plex Sans SemiBold, tracking -1% page titles, login, empty states

"Data is mono" rule: this is the second identity marker after the rail. A commit abc1234, a vpc-0f3a..., a +3 ~1 −0 are always in mono — the eye instantly distinguishes what comes from the system from what comes from the interface. Scale: 13 px base UI (density), 12 px tables and logs, 16/20/24 px titles. No weight beyond SemiBold.

docs.title: 3.4 Spacing, radius, elevation
docs.text:
• 4 px grid. Table cell padding: 6×10 px (dense), forms: 12 px.
  • Radius: 4 px everywhere, 2 px on badges. No pills except state badges.
  • Elevation: no shadows; hierarchy = background (base < surface < raised) + rules.
  • Iconography: Lucide, 16 px, stroke 1.5, always accompanied by a label (never an icon alone on a destructive action).

docs.title: 4. Navigation architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stackd   │ topbar : breadcrumb · health · user      │
│──────────├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▣ Stacks │                                          │
│ ⎇ Graph  │              content                     │
│ ▤ Audit  │   (max width 1440px, tables full-width)  │
│ ▥ Workers│                                          │
│ ⚙ Sets   │                                          │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Labeled side nav (≈ 208 px, icon + text label): Stacks, Graph, Audit, Workers, Variable Sets, Settings, with the StackD mark + wordmark at the top. Active item = brand-violet text + raised background. The product has few sections: no mega-menu.
  • Decision (revised): labels are always visible, not only on hover. An icons-only nav forces recall (guessing what an icon means); a labeled nav plays on recognition — faster, less ambiguous, and better for accessibility (the label is not carried by the aria-label alone). For an expert tool used daily, clarity wins over the 150 px gained. The earlier "56 px icons + tooltip, expandable on hover" track is abandoned: the tooltip hides information behind an interaction.
  • Structural breadcrumb: space / stack / environment / run #142 — always present, each segment clickable. It is the backbone of orientation, given the 4-level hierarchy.
  • ⌘K command palette from v1: go to a stack/env, trigger a run, copy an ID. For an expert audience, this is the real primary navigation; the visual nav is the fallback.
  • Routing: clean, shareable URLs (/stacks/core-network/prod/runs/142?phase=plan&line=87) — a link pasted in Slack during an incident must land exactly at the right place.

docs.title: 5.1 /stacks — the overview (home)
docs.text:
• Dense table, no cards. One row = one stack; columns = environments (dev, staging, prod, in position order).
  • Each env cell = horizontal mini-rail of the last run + relative timestamp + Git lag chip ↑3 (mono, neutral blue-gray — this is information, not a decision: amber stays reserved) when the branch has advanced since the last apply; an attenuated version if the commits do not touch the project_root. Tooltip = list of commits, click = trigger a run. Clickable cell → the env.
  • Sticky header row, sorting, filter by text and by state ("show me everything that is failed or unconfirmed").
  • "Attention required" zone pinned at the top: all unconfirmed and failed runs of the space, across all environments. This is the answer to "what is waiting on a decision?" without searching.

docs.title: 5.2 /runs/{id} — the most important screen
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ core-network / prod / run #142        [Confirm] [Discard]│ ← sticky bar
│ abc1234 "add NAT gateway" · J.Dupont · via cascade       │
├────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RAIL   │  [Plan ±]  [Checks 2✓ 1⚠]  [Logs]  [Inputs]     │
│ of     │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ phases │ │                 tab content                 │ │
│ (§2.2) │ │                                             │ │
└────────┴─┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┴─┘
  • Sticky action bar at the top, not at the bottom: the decision is always visible, with the context (who triggered, env tier). Confirm button amber, disabled with the reason spelled out ("tier prod not in your allowed tiers (dev, staging)", "approver role required", "destroy permission required", "mocked run — apply disabled", "you triggered this prod run"). The triggerer and the confirmer are shown with their tier.
  • Friction proportional to risk. An authorized apply on an ordinary tier = one click. But confirming an apply on a tier flagged requires_four_eyes (the seeded prod) or any destroy run requires an explicit confirmation in a popover anchored to the button: typing the name of the environment (GitHub pattern, consistent with deletions §5.7) + a +a ~c −d summary of the plan, destructions highlighted. Consistent with the principle: deleting a stack already requires typing its name — applying a destruction on prod cannot be less demanding than editing config. The popover bypasses no access rule (can_apply is still evaluated on the API side): it is a misclick safeguard, not a permission check.
  • Staleness banner: if the tracked branch advances while a plan awaits confirmation, a banner above the content — "Plan computed on abc1234 · the branch has advanced by 2 commits" — with a Re-plan action. Confirming remains possible (applying a precise commit is legitimate), but never unknowingly.
  • Header: triggerer AND confirmer shown (Google avatars) — audit is in the interface, not hidden in a page.
  • Plan tab: +3 ~1 −0 summary in giant mono, then a list of resources grouped by action (create/update/delete), each resource expandable into an attribute-by-attribute diff (added green / modified amber / deleted red, values in mono). Destructions are always expanded by default — a delete is never hidden.
  • Checks tab: one block per hook check, from every stage of the plan and apply jobs (check_results.results, SPECS §8.3) — name, stage, status, duration, output; warn = amber with the note "manual confirmation required" (a warning at an apply stage comes after the confirmation and only informs). A run older than results shows its checks instead (warn/fail only), with the stage as —.
  • Inputs tab: resolved variables with their provenance as a mono badge (set:common-aws, stack, env, dependency, MOCK in magenta). Sensitive values: ••• with no "reveal" button.

docs.title: 5.3 Log viewer (in the run page)
docs.text:
• Full screen available (f), bg-base background, JetBrains Mono 12 px, line-height 1.5.
  • Sections collapsible by phase and by hook (chevron + duration + exit code in the section header).
  • Line numbers in the gutter, click = shareable anchor, highlight of the targeted line on arrival.
  • Follow-tail active by default on a run in progress; the slightest scroll up suspends it (floating "↓ Resume following" button with a counter of new lines).
  • Full ANSI rendering (palette mapped onto our tokens, not raw terminal colors). Internal ⌘F search with an occurrence counter. Timestamps toggle. Mandatory virtualization (react-virtuoso).

docs.title: 5.4 /graph and run groups
docs.text:
• react-flow, dagre layout left→right, filter by environment name at the top (see the "prod" graph without the dev noise).
  • Node = minimal card: stack/env + mini-rail of the last run. Edge labeled with the number of output references; dashed magenta edge if mocks are involved.
  • Run group view: same graph, the nodes color in real time during the cascade. No confetti at the end — a green finished state is enough.
  • Mandatory accessible alternative: a react-flow graph is not navigable by screen reader nor by keyboard alone. A systematic "list view" toggle = an adjacency table (upstream env → downstream env · N references · MOCK?) that is sortable, focusable, with the same filter. The graph is the default display; the list is the complete functional equivalent, not a stopgap. The graph nodes remain reachable via Tab (topological order) with an aria-label announcement of the last run's state.
  • Auto-link by name: a collapsible action wires two stacks in bulk — for every same-named env pair it links each matching upstream output to the downstream input of the same name (one POST instead of adding references one by one). Reports the count of references created.

docs.title: 5.5 /queue — the execution queue
docs.text:
The visual answer to "why isn't my run starting?".

  • Two groups: In progress (claimed runs, with worker, active phase and duration) and Waiting (queued + confirmed not claimed), sorted by age.
  • Each waiting run displays its blocking reason computed by the API, spelled out and in mono: run #141 active on this environment, environment locked, no worker compatible with {pool: prod}, apply affinity reservation (worker-aws-1, 38s remaining).
  • Filter by stack/env/pool; direct link to the blocking run and to /workers.
  • A queue counter in the side nav (badge on the icon) when runs have been waiting for > 2 min — a discreet signal, no toast.

docs.title: 5.6 /audit
docs.text:
• Dense chronological table: mono timestamp, avatar + email, action as a badge, target as a clickable breadcrumb, summarized context.
  • The ⭐ actions (run.confirmed, run.applied) have a slightly contrasted row.
  • Combinable filters in a top bar (actor, action, stack, env, period) reflected in the URL → an investigation is shared by link. Discreet CSV export on the right.

docs.title: 5.7 Forms (stack wizard, variables, hooks)
docs.text:
• One column, max 560 px, labels above, help in text-secondary under the field.
  • Every technical name typed (stack, env, variable) is displayed in mono from the first keystroke.
  • Destructive actions require typing the name of the target (GitHub pattern) — not a plain "Are you sure?" modal.
  • Wizard: numbered steps because it is a real sequence; each step independently validatable (the repo check runs at step 1, not at the end).
  • Config list items are uniform (variables, hooks, notifications, secret sources): each is a bordered tile with metadata badges, an edit (pencil) and a delete (trash) affordance. Editing is in place — the tile becomes an inline form, no separate screen. A sensitive value is never pre-filled (write-only): its edit field stays blank with a "leave blank to keep" hint, so toggling hcl/sensitive never clobbers the stored secret. Secret sources expose Rotate token the same way (write-only new bootstrap credential).

docs.title: 5.8 /stacks/{id} — stack & environment configuration
docs.text:
• Two top tabs: Environments (operate) and Settings (configure the stack: general, variables, hooks, notifications, secret sources).
  • Each environment row folds its config behind a single Configure disclosure (progressive disclosure — one panel at a time), with the daily action (Plan) as the sole accent CTA and a discreet refresh HEAD icon (force a re-read of the tracked branch from the remote, updating the stale / ↑N indicators without waiting for the poll).
  • The env Inputs tab has three sections: Resolved (read-only, every value with its provenance badge), Environment overrides (editable env-level variables that override the stack-level value of the same name, SPECS §3.4), and Outputs (what the env publishes after a successful apply — sensitive ones masked, never a reveal button).
  • Discover inputs (on the overrides section): introspects the repo (shallow clone + HCL parse of the root module, no terraform run) and scaffolds the required inputs that aren't already provided as env variables with empty, type-valid placeholders (hcl/sensitive set from the declaration). Already-resolved inputs are skipped.
  • The env Settings tab edits the environment after creation: name, tier, branch, and the protection flags (protected, four-eyes, autodeploy, managed_state, allow_mock_apply, allow_fallback_apply). When managed_state is off, two backend config fields appear — a repo-relative file (-backend-config=<file>) and an inline key/value editor (each → -backend-config=key=value, e.g. bucket/key/region/use_lockfile). For onboarding a new tier on shared code with no per-env .config yet (SPECS §11.3).
  • The branch is per-environment (each env tracks its own), chosen from the repo's real branches at creation (defaults to main).
  • Variable Sets (/variable-sets): each set is a row; Configure folds its config behind a tab bar (one panel at a time, like the env card) — Variables, Attachments (bind to a stack, an environment, or a tier — all envs of that tier — or detach), Settings (rename, auto-attach, and a selector — auto-attach to any stack/env whose labels match). Collapsed, the row stays glanceable: a badge shows how the set reaches envs (auto-attach, or rule: team=payments). auto-attach applies the set to the whole space without an explicit attachment (SPECS §3.4).

docs.title: 5.9 /workers — workers & pools
docs.text:
• Workers grouped by pool (read): per-worker status, labels, last heartbeat, agent version, and Diagnostics / Logs actions.
  • Pool management (admin): list, create and delete worker pools. Creating one mints the agent registration token, surfaced once in a dismissible banner with a copy action — it is hashed at rest and never retrievable again (so the empty-state hint "start an agent with a pool token" is now actionable from the UI).

docs.title: 6. Real-time patterns
docs.text:
• A single multiplexed WebSocket; TanStack Query remains the source of truth (WS events invalidate queries, they do not patch the cache by hand — except logs, which are streamed directly).
  • A run's state change is visible everywhere it appears (rail, badges) without a refresh, via subscription to the topics of the displayed entities.
  • Discreet connection indicator in the topbar; on a disconnect: a thin "Reconnecting…" banner + after_seq catch-up, never a blocking modal.
  • No toast for background events (a run that finishes is seen on its rail). Toasts are reserved for feedback on the current user's actions.

docs.title: 7. Accessibility, states, quality
docs.text:
• Minimum AA contrast on both themes (verified on the state colors over their actual backgrounds).
  • Color is never the sole carrier of state: each badge has its text label, the rail has icons per segment (✓ ✕ ⏸ ▶). Color blindness = the nominal case in this trade.
  • Full keyboard navigation: j/k in tables, f full-screen logs, ⌘K palette, visible brand-violet 2 px focus. prefers-reduced-motion: the rail's pulse becomes a static opacity change.
  • Skip-link "Go to content" as the first focusable element (side nav + breadcrumb = many tab stops before the content on a dense app).
  • Polite live regions, never focus stealing: real-time state changes (rail, badges, "Reconnecting…" banner) are announced via aria-live="polite" and never move the user's focus (they may be reading logs or filling out a form). Action toasts use aria-live and do not capture focus.
  • Tabular figures: font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on any data aligned in a column (durations, +a ~c −d, counters, timestamps) — JetBrains Mono is already monospaced, but we force tabular-nums so the columns do not dance during streaming.
  • Async action buttons: Confirm/Discard/Trigger/Re-plan go into a loading state (spinner + disabled) during the call, to avoid double submission — distinct from the "missing permission" disabled which, for its part, carries the reason.
  • On-call mobile journey: on the two mobile-polished screens (read a run/logs, confirm/discard), touch targets respect a 44 px minimum; elsewhere desktop density prevails.
  • Empty states = invitations to act, in the product's vocabulary: "No stack. Connect a repo to get started." + button. No decorative illustrations.
  • Errors: factual, in clear technical English, with the way out ("The webhook was rejected: invalid HMAC signature. Check the secret in Settings → Webhooks."). Never apologies, never vague.
  • Skeletons faithful to the final shape for tables; spinners reserved for one-off actions.
  • Responsive: optimized for desktop (the trade), but polished mobile consultation for two precise journeys — reading a run/its logs and confirming/discarding (on-call). The rest may degrade.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
• Tailwind v4 + CSS custom-property tokens (--color-bg-base, --color-state-running, ...): the two themes = two sets of variables, components use only the tokens. No hardcoded color in a component.
  • shadcn/ui as the mechanical base (Dialog, Popover, Command, DropdownMenu) fully re-skinned onto our tokens: we keep Radix's accessibility, we replace the default aesthetic (which is precisely the generic look we refuse).
  • In-house components (the identity core): <PhaseRail> (+ mini variant), <StateBadge>, <LogViewer>, <PlanDiff>, <ProvenanceBadge>, <RunActionBar>, <EnvCell>.
  • Storybook (or Ladle) from Phase 0 for these components: it is the visual contract that Claude Code must respect when building the pages.
  • Self-hosted fonts (IBM Plex Sans, JetBrains Mono) — the app can run on a private network without an external CDN. font-display: swap, preload of only the critical weights (Sans 400/600, Mono 400), fallback metrics (size-adjust/ascent-override) to avoid CLS on load.
  • Theme preference without browser storage (product invariant: neither localStorage nor sessionStorage). Consequence: the theme follows prefers-color-scheme by default; a manual override lives in memory (lost on reload) and, if per-user persistence is desired, it is stored server-side on the profile (GET /me), never in the browser. To be settled when building the topbar (theme toggle).
  • Graphs: react-flow + dagre. Logs: ANSI rendering (anser planned; current LogViewer renders without react-virtuoso). Dates: native Intl, relative format < 24 h then absolute local ISO.
  • Bundle & tests (Phase G): route-level React.lazy/Suspense per page + Vite manualChunks isolating the graph stack (@xyflow/react + dagre + d3, deferred to /graph) and a long-cached react-vendor chunk. Initial JS ≈ 95 KB gz (index + react-vendor), well under the 250 KB target; the ~90 KB-gz graph chunk loads only on /graph. Testing: vitest (pnpm test = vitest run, jsdom) for the identity components (StateBadge, ProvenanceBadge) and pure logic (parseProvenance); one Playwright happy path (pnpm e2e: dev-login → Stacks) as a CI job against task dev. task test now actually runs the front unit tests (the prior --run flag was silently swallowed).

docs.title: 9. What we forbid ourselves (reminder)
docs.text:
• Drop shadows, gradients, glassmorphism, decorative illustrations, emojis in the UI.
  • State colors used for anything other than state; brand violet used to carry state meaning; amber used outside its meaning ("needs a human": decision, unconfirmed, warn/review signals) — e.g. for log severity or technical telemetry.
  • An icon alone on a destructive action; confirmation without typing the name for deletions and for any apply on a requires_four_eyes tier or any destroy apply (§5.2).
  • Toasts for background events; unsolicited animations beyond the rail's pulse.
  • Hiding or collapsing a resource destruction in a plan.
  • Any system text (ID, SHA, value, duration) in the UI font: data is mono, always.

docs.title: DEV.md — Local development mode
docs.text: Goal: git clone → task dev → test a complete plan → confirm → apply → cascade cycle in under 5 minutes, without a Google account, without AWS, without a GitHub repo.

docs.title: 1. Principle: everything is real, except the external boundaries
docs.text:
Dev mode runs the real components (API, scheduler, state machine, worker, state backend, audit) and replaces only the three external dependencies:

Dependency In prod In local dev Google auth OIDC accounts.google.com Dev login flag-gated (§3) Git repos GitHub/GitLab Local fixture repos file:// + optional Gitea (§4) AWS cloud Real STS/providers Cloud-less fixtures (built-in terraform_data, no provider) + optional LocalStack (§6)

Everything else (Postgres, Garage, the worker protocol, hooks, mocks, staleness) works identically to prod. This is intentional: dev mode tests the platform, not a simulation of the platform.

docs.title: 2. Docker compose stack
docs.text:
# deploy/docker-compose.dev.yml
services:
  postgres:        # 18, port 5432, named volume
  garage:          # local S3 (Garage), S3 API on :3900, admin CLI `garage` ; layout, key and stackd bucket provisioned by `task dev`
  api:             # uv run uvicorn --reload, mounts ./api, port 8000
  front:           # vite dev server, mounts ./front, port 5173, proxy /api → api
  worker:          # agent in --reload mode (watchfiles), runner=local (§5)
  # optional profiles:
  gitea:           # profile "git"  : real webhooks locally (§4)
  localstack:      # profile "aws"  : simulated S3/RDS/IAM (§6)

task dev            # S3 bootstrap + compose up (base services) + migrations + seed
task dev-git        # + Gitea (webhook testing)
task dev-aws        # + LocalStack
task seed           # (re)creates the demo data, idempotent
task s3             # provision the dev S3 (Garage layout, key into .env, bucket), idempotent; part of dev
task s3-ls          # list the dev bucket (managed states, saved plans)
task reset          # down -v, drop .dev/pool.token, then dev : start from scratch
task logs           # aggregated colored logs (api, worker)
task test           # pytest + vitest
task e2e            # complete automated scenario (§7)

Orchestration via Task (Taskfile.yml at the root) rather than Make: readable YAML syntax, cross-platform (single Go binary, no dependency on GNU Make), native deps/status for idempotence, namespaces per module, and self-documented task --list. Excerpt:

# Taskfile.yml
version: '3'
dotenv: ['.env']
vars:
  COMPOSE: docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.dev.yml

tasks:
  dev:
    desc: Complete local stack (compose + S3 bootstrap + migrations + seed)
    deps: [env]
    cmds:
      - task: s3                    # before `up`: compose reads the S3 key from .env at creation
      - "{{.COMPOSE}} up -d --wait"
      - task: migrate
      - task: seed-fixtures
      - task: seed

  s3:
    desc: Provision the dev S3 (Garage layout, access key into .env, bucket; idempotent)
    cmds: [bash scripts/bootstrap-s3.sh]

  env:
    desc: Generates .env and dev keys on first launch
    cmds: [bash scripts/bootstrap-env.sh]
    status: [test -f .env]          # idempotent: does nothing if .env exists

  seed:
    desc: Demo data (idempotent)
    cmds: ["{{.COMPOSE}} exec -T api uv run python -m app.seed"]

  reset:
    desc: Tear everything down and start fresh
    cmds:
      - "{{.COMPOSE}} down -v"
      - rm -f .dev/pool.token       # belongs to the wiped DB: the worker waits for the new seed's
      - task: dev

  push-change:
    desc: Simulates a merge into demo-network (staleness test)
    dir: .dev/repos/demo-network
    cmds:
      - date >> CHANGELOG.txt
      # Quote the whole command — the ": " in the message is a YAML mapping token otherwise.
      - 'git add -A && git commit -m "feat: simulated merge"'

  e2e:
    desc: Complete §7 scenario (non-regression)
    deps: [dev]
    cmds: ["{{.COMPOSE}} exec -T api uv run pytest e2e -v"]

.env.example → .env copied automatically by task dev (task env, scripts/bootstrap-env.sh, only when .env is missing): dev keys (encryption key, JWT secret, OIDC keypair) generated on first launch and stored in .dev/ (gitignored), the first two injected into .env. No secret value committed, no manual entry.

Dev S3 (Garage): the API keeps managed states and every tracked/destroy run's saved plan (encrypted; deleted when the run ends) in S3, so a plan with changes needs a provisioned Garage. task s3 (scripts/bootstrap-s3.sh, run by every dev* task) brings garage up and, checking before each step:

  1. assigns the single-node layout (zone dc1) and applies it;
  2. writes a generated access key into .env (S3_ACCESS_KEY / S3_SECRET_KEY) only when both are empty, then imports it into Garage if Garage lacks it;
  3. creates the S3_BUCKET bucket (stackd) and grants the key read/write/owner on it.

A re-run changes nothing. Compose reads .env when it creates a container, which is why task dev runs the bootstrap before up; a stack started before the key existed is recreated by that up, since its .env values changed. Garage binds IPv4 (0.0.0.0, deploy/garage.toml), so it also starts on hosts whose kernel has IPv6 disabled. The CI e2e workflow runs the same script.

Only the api holds platform secrets. The S3 key, DATABASE_URL, STACKD_ENCRYPTION_KEY, STACKD_JWT_SECRET and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET come from the shared .env, and compose blanks all of them in the worker's environment: the worker reaches plans and states through the API (SPECS §11.1) and needs none of them, and tofu and platform hooks inherit the worker's environment (minus its own STACKD_* settings) — repo code runs inside tofu. Repo hooks only get an allowlist of it (SPECS §8.3).

task reset runs down -v (Postgres and Garage volumes), deletes .dev/pool.token, then task dev. .env and .dev/ keys are kept, so the S3 bootstrap imports the same key into the fresh Garage. The pool token belongs to the wiped database: without it the worker waits (re-reading the file) for the new seed's token instead of registering with a stale one before the migrations have run.

docs.title: 3. Auth in dev: the dev login
docs.text:
Running the real Google flow locally is possible (OAuth client with redirect http://localhost:8000) but cumbersome for quick testing. Dev mode therefore adds an explicitly gated bypass:

STACKD_DEV_AUTH=true        # rejected if STACKD_ENV=production (assert at startup)
  • The login page displays, below the Google button, a "Dev login" panel with three personas covering the permissions in SPECS §2.4: admin@dev.local (admin, tiers dev/staging/prod, destroy), alice@dev.local (approver, tiers dev/staging/prod), bob@dev.local (writer, tiers dev/staging — a writer cannot confirm any apply). One click = session.
  • Three personas: essential for testing the role gate (bob triggers, but is refused at confirm everywhere), prod 4-eyes (bob triggers, alice confirms) and audit ("who applied what" only makes sense with several people). No persona is an approver without prod, so the "apply everywhere except prod" tier gate needs a space membership (PUT /api/v1/spaces/{id}/members) giving an approver {dev, staging}.
  • Sessions, roles and audit events are strictly the same as with Google — only the google_sub is synthetic (dev:admin).
  • The real Google flow remains testable in dev by setting GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/SECRET (the two coexist).

Safeguard: the prod build of the API image removes the dev_auth module (not just the flag) — a configuration oversight cannot expose the bypass.

docs.title: 4. Git fixture repos
docs.text:
task seed-fixtures (scripts/seed-fixtures.sh, run on the host by every dev* task, idempotent) creates in .dev/repos/ two local and committable Git repositories (branch main). They use only the built-in terraform_data resource: no provider to download, tofu plan/apply runs fully offline.

.dev/repos/demo-network/      # upstream stack
  main.tf                     #   variable org, terraform_data "network", output network_name
.dev/repos/demo-app/          # downstream stack
  main.tf                     #   variables org + network_name, terraform_data "app", output app_target
  • The seed stacks point to them with repo_url: file:///stackd-dev/repos/demo-network (.dev/ is mounted at /stackd-dev in the API and the worker; STACKD_SEED_REPO_BASE overrides the base). repo_auth_kind: none. The fixtures carry no .stackd.yml.
  • Simulate "a PR is merged" without GitHub: task push-change commits a change in demo-network → staleness polling (reduced to 15 s in dev via STACKD_HEAD_POLL_INTERVAL) turns stale to true (GET /api/v1/environments/{id}) on an env that already has a finished tracked run. The ↑1 chip of DESIGN §5.1 is not in the UI yet. Perfect for testing the "apply at 9am, merge at 9:15am" scenario.
  • Real webhooks: task dev-git launches Gitea (profile git, port 3000). Pushing the fixtures to it and configuring its webhook to the API are manual for now (no seed-gitea or webhook task yet).

docs.title: 5. Worker in dev
docs.text:
• Launched by compose with STACKD_RUNNER=local: terraform commands run directly inside the worker container (image including OpenTofu + jq + git). No Docker-in-Docker — the docker runner is not implemented in the agent yet (SPECS §7.4), so there is nothing to exercise in dev.
  • Tool binaries: OpenTofu and Terraform pre-installed in the dev image (no download on first run). A stack's tool picks which one runs — no separate "terraform worker", any dev worker handles both.
  • Agent hot reload (watchfiles): modifying worker/ cleanly restarts the poll loop (the current job finishes).
  • Multi-workers to test concurrency and affinity: docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.dev.yml up -d --scale worker=3, or STACKD_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS for several jobs per worker.
  • The worker reads its pool token from .dev/pool.token (STACKD_POOL_TOKEN_FILE), written by the seed: it waits for the file and re-reads it on a failed registration.

docs.title: 6. Terraform without AWS (and with, if needed)
docs.text:
By default: the fixtures use only the built-in terraform_data resource — zero providers, zero credentials, zero cost, execution in seconds. Enough to test the entire platform (the platform orchestrates terraform, it does not depend on what terraform creates).

aws profile (LocalStack): to test AWS-realistic stacks (S3, SQS, IAM...), task dev-aws brings up LocalStack on :4566; the seed creates no LocalStack variable set, so add the provider endpoint overrides yourself (e.g. in a variable set). Known limitations: LocalStack does not cover everything and does not validate workload OIDC (STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is superficial there).
