docs.title: Exit & data portability
docs.text: Stackd is designed for low lock-in. It's self-hosted (no SaaS holds your data), your IaC stays in your Git repos, your state is plain tfstate, and your cloud access is standard IAM. The real question isn't "vendor lock-in" — it's switching cost, and it's small. This page documents exactly how to leave and get everything back.

docs.title: What is never captive
docs.text: Data Where it lives Getting it back Your IaC code your Git repos Stackd only references repo_url@commit — the code never moved. State (managed_state: false) your own S3/backend Stackd never touches it. Stop using Stackd; tofu keeps working against your backend. No migration. State (managed_state: true) Stackd's S3, standard tfstate format Pull it out via the HTTP backend (below). No proprietary format. Cloud credentials your cloud account (IAM OIDC provider + roles) Standard IAM — delete or repoint anytime. Repo hooks your repo (.stackd.yml) Versioned with your code.

docs.title: What lives only in Stackd (but is exportable)
docs.text:
• Orchestration config — stacks, environments, tiers, dependencies, variable sets. Exportable via the API (GET /stacks, /environments/{id}, /graph, /environments/{id}/resolved-variables). Re-creatable; it isn't infrastructure.
  • History — runs, logs, audit. The audit trail exports to CSV (GET /api/v1/audit/export).
  • Sensitive variable values — write-only by design (AES-GCM, never returned in clear). Keep your own source of truth for secrets — you should anyway. Non-sensitive values come back via /resolved-variables.

Want zero state exit cost?

Stay on managed_state: false. You get the full orchestration (plan → approval → apply, audit, OIDC, cascade) while your state stays entirely in your own backend — nothing to migrate if you ever leave.

docs.title: The exit procedure (rollback)
docs.text: This is the exact reverse of importing an existing stack.

docs.title: 1. Pull managed state back out
docs.text:
Only for environments with managed_state: true. Mint a session (admin; it returns a scoped rw token + the HTTP backend config, valid 30 minutes). In a local checkout, add a terraform { backend "http" {} } block, export the session's settings as TF_HTTP_* variables (exactly as in importing, step 3) and run tofu init. Then:

# get a scoped token + backend address
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV_ID/state/import-session -H "$AUTH"

# option A — pull the raw tfstate (it's standard) and push it anywhere
tofu state pull > terraform.tfstate

# option B — migrate in place: replace the `http` backend block with your own
# (`s3`, local…), then:
tofu init -migrate-state

docs.title: 2. Repoint terraform / CI at the repos directly
docs.text: Your code never moved — point your existing CI or local tofu at the repos and backends and you're running on your own again.

docs.title: 3. Re-supply variables & secrets
docs.text: Export the non-sensitive resolved variables; re-provide sensitive ones from your own secret store (Stackd can't hand them back in clear — by design).

docs.title: 4. (Optional) Archive config & audit
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/audit/export -H "$AUTH" > audit.csv
curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks -H "$AUTH" > stacks.json

docs.title: 5. Decommission
docs.text: Delete the IAM OIDC provider + roles in your cloud account if you no longer want them, then stop Stackd.

docs.title: The bottom line
docs.text: At any moment, tofu alone against your state is enough to take back control. The only real exit work is migrating managed state (one standard tofu init -migrate-state, fully reversible) and re-creating the orchestration config elsewhere — neither touches your infrastructure.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The product's flow is plan → human confirmation → apply. Notifications make sure the human actually learns a decision is waiting — without staring at the UI.

A notification target is an outbound webhook attached to a stack or an environment (exactly like a platform hook). It fires when a run enters one of a chosen set of states.

docs.title: When notifications fire
docs.text:
state when it fires typical use unconfirmed a plan is ready and awaits confirmation ping the approver: "prod apply waiting" failed a run failed alert on breakage finished a run finished (incl. apply) deploy log / changelog

Default on_states is ["unconfirmed", "failed"]; those three states are the only accepted values. Two kinds exist: slack posts {"text": …} to a Slack/Mattermost incoming webhook (with a deep link to the run), and webhook posts a structured JSON envelope (state, run id, run type, stack/env, tier, commit, url). Deep links use STACKD_APP_URL, the SPA base.

docs.title: Setting up Slack
docs.text:
The slack kind posts to a Slack incoming webhook — a URL Slack gives you that drops a message into one channel. No bot token, no scopes.

  1. Go to api.slack.com/apps → Create New App → From scratch, pick your workspace.
  2. Open Incoming Webhooks and toggle it On.
  3. Add New Webhook to Workspace, choose the target channel, Allow.
  4. Copy the URL — it looks like https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX. That's the url you give Stackd.

Mattermost incoming webhooks accept the same {"text": …} payload — use the slack kind with the Mattermost URL.

Verify before you rely on it

After creating a target, hit test (UI) or POST …/notifications/{id}/test (API). It delivers a message explicitly flagged as a test (🧪 … (test) for Slack, {"event":"notification.test","test":true} for a webhook), so you can confirm the URL works without waiting for a real run — and no one mistakes it for a real event.

docs.title: Setting up a generic webhook
docs.text:
The webhook kind POSTs the JSON envelope (see below) to any HTTPS endpoint you control (a CI bridge, a Lambda URL, an internal service).

  • Method/format: POST, Content-Type: application/json.
  • No signature: outbound notification webhooks are not HMAC-signed (unlike inbound GitHub webhooks, which use stacks.webhook_secret). Treat the URL itself as the secret — use an unguessable path or a token your receiver checks. The URL must be https on a public host (see Network requirements).
  • Idempotency: delivery is at-least-once (see Delivery guarantees); key on run_id + state so a retry is a no-op.

docs.title: Ping the approver when a prod plan is waiting
docs.text:
Attach a Slack target to a production environment. It pings on unconfirmed (something to approve) and on failed:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV_ID/notifications \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
    "name": "prod-approvals",
    "kind": "slack",
    "url": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ",
    "on_states": ["unconfirmed", "failed"],
    "enabled": true
  }'

The Slack message carries a deep link straight to the run awaiting confirmation — see Runs & approvals.

docs.title: A generic webhook target
docs.text:
Attach a structured-envelope target to a whole stack (it covers every environment of that stack):

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK_ID/notifications \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
    "name": "ci-bridge",
    "kind": "webhook",
    "url": "https://ci.example.com/hooks/stackd",
    "on_states": ["finished", "failed"],
    "enabled": true
  }'

The webhook kind POSTs a JSON envelope:

{
  "event": "run.state_changed",
  "state": "finished",
  "run_id": "0190e...c3",
  "run_type": "tracked",
  "stack": "payments",
  "environment": "payments-prod",
  "tier": "prod",
  "commit_sha": "a1b2c3d4e5f6...",
  "url": "http://localhost:5173/runs/0190e...c3"
}

docs.title: Managing targets
docs.text:
Both scopes expose the same CRUD. List or create on the scope, then patch or delete by target id:

curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK_ID/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -s -X PATCH localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV_ID/notifications/$TARGET_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"enabled": false}'
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK_ID/notifications/$TARGET_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

For a run's env, both the env-level and the stack-level targets resolve and fire (filtered by on_states). Deleting a stack or an environment deletes its targets too (each audited notification_target.deleted with the reason).

docs.title: Network requirements and SSRF protection
docs.text:
Targets are URLs that users enter and the API POSTs to from inside your network, so Stackd guards against server-side request forgery:

  • The URL must use https, and its host must resolve to public addresses only: a private, loopback, link-local (including the 169.254.169.254 metadata endpoint), reserved or multicast address is refused with a 422 at create/update, and checked again at every delivery.
  • At delivery the API resolves the host once, vets every address, then connects to a vetted IP directly. The Host header, TLS SNI and certificate verification still use the hostname. This closes the DNS-rebinding window between the check and the connection.
  • Redirects are not followed; the request times out after 5 s.
  • Proxy settings are ignored by design. Delivery never goes through HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or any other environment proxy: a proxy would resolve the hostname again, which would defeat the pinning.

Egress through a proxy only

If the API's only route to the internet is an HTTP proxy, notifications cannot be delivered: the API needs direct outbound HTTPS (port 443) to the target hosts, for example through a NAT gateway or a firewall allow rule for hooks.slack.com. A relay on your private network does not help either, since private addresses are refused. Failed deliveries are retried, then logged (see below); the test button surfaces the error immediately.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
Notifications are not a fire-and-forget side effect. When a run transitions to a notify-worthy state, a row is inserted into the outbox in the same DB transaction as the state change — no HTTP in the request path. A background scheduler drains the outbox under an advisory lock (one replica at a time) and POSTs to the matching targets.

Note

Delivery is at-least-once. The outbox is drained under a pg_try_advisory_lock with SKIP LOCKED, so two API replicas never double-send — but a receiver may still see a retry, so make handlers idempotent. A rolled-back transition never notifies (its outbox row rolls back too). Failed deliveries retry up to 5 times, then dead-letter and log; a flaky Slack never blocks or fails a run.

docs.title: Observability: health, logs & diagnostics
docs.text: Stackd is built so that one page and one endpoint answer the question "is the platform healthy, and if not, why?". Health is a single live snapshot; logs are a structured, filterable buffer; worker diagnostics let you debug a remote agent without opening a shell. This page is task-oriented — pick the section that matches what you're trying to find out.

docs.title: Health at a glance
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/health (any signed-in user) returns one snapshot: a DB connectivity check, workers (online / total, and each worker's pool, labels, status and last heartbeat), runs (active / queued), and how many warnings and errors the log buffer holds. The front Workers & health page renders this snapshot alongside a live logs panel, and a green/red status dot sits in the topbar so you see degradation without leaving your current screen.

curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/health -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

{
  "status": "ok",
  "env": "development",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "checks": { "database": "ok" },
  "workers": {
    "total": 1,
    "online": 1,
    "items": [
      { "name": "worker-1", "pool": "local", "labels": null, "status": "idle", "online": true,
        "last_heartbeat_at": "2026-10-10T09:31:02+00:00", "seconds_since_heartbeat": 3.2 }
    ]
  },
  "runs": { "active": 1, "queued": 4 },
  "log_buffer": { "size": 812, "recent_warn_error": 3 }
}

status turns degraded when the database check fails. A worker whose heartbeat is older than 60 s shows as offline; see Workers & scaling for the worker-lost lifecycle (only runs executing on a lost worker are failed).

Two unauthenticated endpoints sit outside /api/v1 for probes and scrapers: GET /healthz (liveness) and GET /metrics (Prometheus: runs by state, queue depth, workers online, claim latency, run duration, webhook results — counts only, never secrets). Restrict /metrics at the network layer.

docs.title: Querying logs
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/logs (admin only) serves the structured JSON ring buffer. Filter by level, event, worker_id, run_id, request_id, or free-text q. Every HTTP response carries an X-Request-ID header, so you can copy it from a failing call and correlate that request across all the log lines it produced.

# Everything that happened for one request
curl -s "localhost:8000/api/v1/logs?request_id=01J7Z…" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Errors touching a specific run
curl -s "localhost:8000/api/v1/logs?run_id=$RUN_ID&level=ERROR" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Log levels carry signal, not volume
docs.text:
Levels are chosen so that the default stream is the interesting stream:

  • INFO — mutations and domain events (run.transition, worker.claim, …).
  • DEBUG — reads, polls and heartbeats. Hidden by default (they're noise).
  • WARNING — all 4xx responses.
  • ERROR — all 5xx responses.

Set STACKD_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG to surface the polls and heartbeats too when you're chasing something low-level.

docs.title: Worker diagnostics
docs.text:
From the Workers & health page, a per-worker button queues a read-only debug bundle: tool versions, disk usage, environment variable names, and recent agent logs. There is no inbound connection to a worker — the request is delivered over the heartbeat command channel (the worker pulls it on its next 20 s beat) and the result comes back via POST /worker/v1/commands/{id}/result.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/workers/$WORKER_ID/diagnostics -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# then read it back once the worker has answered:
curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/workers/$WORKER_ID/diagnostics -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Diagnostics expose names, never values

The bundle lists environment variable names only — never their values. Secrets are never logged anywhere: sensitive variables are masked by the agent and never appear in logs, health output, or a diagnostics bundle.

docs.title: Inspecting object storage (dev)
docs.text: Managed states and saved plans live in S3 (Garage in dev), reached only by the API. task s3-ls lists the dev bucket with the API's own S3 settings: states/<environment_id>/… for state versions, artifacts/<run_id>/plan.tfplan for the saved plan of a run that can still be applied (encrypted, deleted when the run ends). If a plan with changes fails while uploading its plan file, the API cannot reach the bucket: run task s3, then task dev. See Dev environment §2.

docs.title: Watching a run live
docs.text: You don't need to poll for an active run. The run page and the dependency graph subscribe over WebSocket: state transitions, new log lines, and graph status update in place as the worker reports them.

docs.title: Runs & approvals
docs.text: A run is one execution against one environment. It always pauses for a human between plan and apply — that approval gate, and who's allowed through it, is the heart of Stackd.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
queued → preparing → planning → [checking] → unconfirmed → confirmed → applying → finished

A worker claims a queued run and executes its plan job: it clones the repo, runs hooks + plan, and reports back. With a non-empty diff the run stops at unconfirmed and waits for a human. After confirm, a worker (not necessarily the same one) claims the apply job and drives the run to finished. An empty diff goes straight to finished; a failure to failed. A human can discard an unconfirmed run, or cancel a queued or unconfirmed one (stopping a run a worker is executing is not supported yet).

Note

State only ever changes through one function (transition()), which records a run_event and — for human/terminal actions — an audit_event in the same transaction. Nothing changes a run's state out of band.

docs.title: What gets applied is what was reviewed
docs.text:
Two guarantees tie the apply to the plan a human approved:

  • The run is pinned to a commit. A run triggered without a commit (a click, a cascade) plans the head of the environment's branch, and the plan job reports the exact commit it checked out: the run is pinned to it. A run triggered on a branch or tag name is pinned to the commit that name resolved to; a run triggered on a full SHA must check out exactly that commit, or it fails (commit_mismatch). The apply clones exactly the pinned commit, so its hooks and output -json run on the reviewed code too, and staleness knows what was applied.
  • The apply runs the saved plan. For a tracked or destroy run with changes, the plan job uploads its plan.tfplan before any after_plan hook runs. The API encrypts it and keeps it in S3 while the run can still be applied. The apply job downloads it and runs tofu apply plan.tfplan — it never re-plans. If the saved plan is missing or unreadable, the run fails before the before_apply hooks (saved plan unavailable, not applied). If the state or an input changed since the plan, tofu refuses the stale plan and the run fails with tofu's reason. In both cases, trigger a new plan. The saved plan is deleted as soon as the run ends, whatever the outcome.

A plan file holds the run's variable values, sensitive ones included: it is encrypted with the API's key on top of the bucket's encryption, written 0600 on the apply worker, and removed right after the apply (the after_apply hooks never see it).

docs.title: Who can approve — can_apply
docs.text:
Confirming an apply requires both:

  1. Role ∈ {approver, admin} — a writer may trigger a plan but never approve.
  2. The environment's tier is in your allowed_tiers set. Tiers are a configurable catalog (not an ordered dev<staging<prod), so a grant can be non-contiguous — e.g. {dev, prod} confirms in dev and prod but not staging.

A destroy run additionally requires the can_destroy permission. A tier flagged requires_four_eyes (e.g. prod) also forces the triggerer ≠ the confirmer.

These are your effective permissions in the environment's space: a space membership can set a different role, tier set or destroy right than your instance defaults.

Persona Can trigger a plan Can approve dev/staging Can approve prod writer (bob) ✅ ❌ (needs approver) ❌ approver with {dev, staging} ✅ ✅ ❌ (tier) approver/admin with prod in their set (alice, admin) ✅ ✅ ✅

docs.title: Four-eyes
docs.text: On an environment whose tier is flagged requires_four_eyes (the seeded prod), a protected environment, or any env with require_second_pair_of_eyes, the person who triggered the run cannot be the one who confirms it — another authorized approver must. It only applies to runs a human triggered: a webhook or cascade run has no triggerer to oppose, so any authorized approver can confirm it.

docs.title: Friction proportional to risk
docs.text: An authorized apply on an ordinary tier is one click. Confirming on a tier flagged requires_four_eyes or any destroy run opens a confirmation popover: type the environment name + review a +a ~c −d plan summary. This is a misclick safeguard only — it never bypasses can_apply (still evaluated server-side).

docs.title: Autodeploy & checks
docs.text:
An environment with autodeploy auto-confirms when the plan is clean — but a warn check forces unconfirmed so a human still sees it. A protected environment can never autodeploy, and requires four-eyes.

Every hook result is kept on the run with the stage it ran at, from the plan job and then the apply job: check_results.results lists them all (ok, warn, fail) — what the run page shows, with each one's stage — and check_results.checks only the ones that warned or failed. A fail check fails the run at its stage; a failing before_apply check means nothing is applied. See Hooks — check results.

docs.title: Mock block
docs.text: A run that consumed a mock upstream output (used_mocks=true) cannot be applied unless the env sets allow_mock_apply=true — see Dependencies & mocks.

docs.title: Promotion (trunk-based)
docs.text:
To roll out the exact commit running on one environment to another of the same stack (dev → staging → prod), use promote — the env's Promote tab, or:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$STAGING_ID/promote -H "$AUTH" \
  -d '{"from_environment_id": "'$DEV_ID'"}'

It pins a new tracked run on the target to the source's last applied commit, so you deploy what was tested — not whatever HEAD happens to be. The apply is gated as usual (tier + four-eyes) at confirm. This is the same-stack counterpart to the cross-stack cascade.

docs.title: Proposed runs (from a PR)
docs.text:
A pull request triggers a proposed run: plan-only, with a read-only state token — a preview that is never applied and saves no plan file. See the Git integration in SPECS.

A pull request's code runs inside tofu (data "external", provisioners), and nobody has reviewed it yet: a proposed run gets none of the environment's secrets. No sensitive variable, of either kind, and no external secret (not even fetched) reaches its job. What a plan needs stays: the cloud credentials of the plan role, read-only by design (see Cloud credentials), the read-only state token and the repo token to clone.

What a proposed run still reaches

A plan that needs a secret gets no value for it: tofu uses the variable's default, or fails with No value for required variable. Plan with credentials that need no static secret (the OIDC plan role) for pull requests to plan. The pull request's code can still read the state (secrets a resource keeps there included) and use the plan role: keep that role read-only and away from secret stores. A per-environment opt-in giving proposed runs the secrets is specified but not implemented. A drift check is a proposed run too, of the last applied commit: it keeps the secrets.

docs.title: Triggering over the API
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV_ID/runs -H "$AUTH" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}'                                         # trigger plan
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/confirm -H "$AUTH"                 # approve → apply
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/discard -H "$AUTH"                 # discard

docs.title: Stacks & environments
docs.text: A stack is a template (a Git repo + a folder + a tool); an environment is an executable instance of that template with its own state, variables and protections. This page shows how to define both via the API.

docs.title: The mental model: template vs instance
docs.text:
Stack Environment Is the template (code) an instance (a deployable target) Holds repo_url, project_root, tool, tool_version, repo auth tier, branch, state, variables, protections, labels Runs? never a run always belongs to an environment

A stack carries no branch, no state, no autodeploy — all of that lives on the environment. See Concepts §2.

docs.title: Defining a stack
docs.text:
A stack points at a Git repo, a subfolder within it (project_root, default .), and the IaC tool. Repo auth is one of none, token, or deploy_key.

STACK=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"core-network","repo_url":"https://github.com/acme/infra.git",
       "project_root":"network","tool":"opentofu","tool_version":"1.12.0"}' | jq -r .id)

One repo, several stacks

A single repo can host many stacks by giving each a distinct project_root (e.g. network, db, app). The push webhook is configured per repo with one shared secret; on receipt the API resolves matching stacks and filters environments by branch and project_root. See SPECS §3.1.

docs.title: Validating the repo
docs.text:
Before creating environments, check that Stackd can reach the repo with the configured auth:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/check-repo \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Defining environments
docs.text:
Each environment is an instance of the stack. The same code runs against physically separate state and variables.

# dev — permissive
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/environments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"dev","tier":"dev","branch":"main"}'

# prod — protected, second pair of eyes
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/environments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"prod","tier":"prod","branch":"main",
       "protected":true,"require_second_pair_of_eyes":true}'

docs.title: Fields that matter
docs.text:
• tier (a configurable catalog, e.g. dev/staging/prod/qa) — carries apply/destroy permissions: can_apply requires env.tier ∈ user.allowed_tiers. See Runs & approvals.
  • branch — the branch this environment tracks for staleness and webhook-driven runs.
  • protected — forces confirmation (never autodeploys) and four-eyes; it is not the access control (that is tier).
  • require_second_pair_of_eyes — four-eyes alone: the person who triggered a run cannot confirm it, and the environment may still autodeploy (already implied on a tier flagged requires_four_eyes, like the seeded prod, and on a protected environment; useful on staging).
  • managed_state — when true, Terraform talks to Stackd's HTTP backend (state bytes in S3) and the repo must declare no backend block: the worker adds backend "http" {} itself. Set false to keep your own backend "s3". See Concepts §8.
  • allow_mock_apply — allow applying a run that consumed mock outputs (default false). See Dependencies & mocks.
  • labels — JSON tags used to target a worker pool.

Why not Terraform workspaces

Workspaces share code, backend and credentials and only suffix the state key — easy to target the wrong one. A Stackd environment is physically isolated: its own state, variables, protections and worker pool.

docs.title: Refreshing the tracked head
docs.text:
Staleness compares the commit of the last finished tracked run (every run is pinned to the commit it planned) to the branch head. head_sha updates via the push webhook or the 15-min git ls-remote polling; force it manually (audited environment.head_refreshed):

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV/refresh-head \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

GET /api/v1/environments/{id} then exposes head_sha, commits_ahead, affects_project_root and stale. An environment with nothing applied yet is never stale. Changing an environment's branch clears its recorded head until the next poll, and a push that deletes the branch clears it too. See SPECS §9.6.

docs.title: Deleting a stack or an environment
docs.text:
DELETE /api/v1/stacks/{id} and DELETE /api/v1/environments/{id} are refused with 409 Active run while one of the environments involved has a run in an active state (preparing through applying, or a command running); the problem body names the run_id. Cancel or discard it, or let it finish, then retry. Queued runs are deleted with their environment.

The deletion also removes, in the same transaction and each audited with the reason (stack_deleted or environment_deleted), everything that points at the stack or its environments:

  • variable-set attachments (variable_set.detached) — the set itself stays;
  • platform hooks (hook.deleted);
  • notification targets (notification_target.deleted).

An attach racing the deletion either fails with 404 or is removed with the rest: no orphan is left behind.

docs.title: Variables & secrets
docs.text: Stackd composes the configuration of every run from layers. The same variable name can be defined in several places; the most specific layer wins, and every resolved value carries its provenance so you can see where it came from.

docs.title: The two kinds
docs.text:
Each variable has a kind that decides how the worker injects it:

Kind Injection terraform written to an auto-loaded tfvars file, present only while a tofu command runs (listed as TF_VAR_<name>); hooks only see it inside plan.json environment exposed as a plain process environment variable for the run: to tofu and hooks — to repo hooks only when it is not sensitive

docs.title: Where a variable can live
docs.text:
• Stack variable — common to all environments of a stack (environment_id is null).
  • Environment variable — scoped to a single environment.
  • Variable set — a named, reusable bundle (e.g. common-aws, datadog, region-eu) that belongs to one space and that you attach to tiers, stacks or envs of that space. Set members are never scoped to an env directly; the attachment carries the targeting.

docs.title: Resolution order (6 layers)
docs.text:
At claim time the value of each variable is resolved from weakest to strongest. The strongest layer that defines a given (name, kind) wins.

flowchart LR
  A["1· sets by rule<br/>(auto_attach, selector)"] --> T["2· sets attached to tier"]
  T --> B["3· sets attached to stack"]
  B --> C["4· sets attached to env"]
  C --> D["5· stack variables"]
  D --> E["6· environment variables<br/>(always wins)"]
Layer Source Ordered by 1 variable sets that apply by rule: auto_attach, or a selector matching the env's labels set name 2 variable sets attached to the env's tier increasing priority 3 variable sets attached to the stack increasing priority 4 variable sets attached to the env increasing priority 5 stack variables — 6 environment variables — (always wins)

Only sets of the environment's own space take part. A selector ({"label": "value", …}) matches an env whose effective labels (stack labels + env labels, env wins) contain every pair. Two more sources are merged in at claim time but sit outside this order: upstream outputs (dependency:) and mocks (mock) — see Concepts and SPECS §9.

docs.title: Inspecting resolved values
docs.text:
GET /environments/{id}/resolved-variables returns the fully resolved set, each entry tagged with its injected_name and provenance:

curl -s localhost:8000/api/v1/environments/$ENV/resolved-variables \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq

[
  { "name": "region", "injected_name": "TF_VAR_region", "value": "us-east-1", "provenance": "set:region-us" },
  { "name": "cidr",   "injected_name": "TF_VAR_cidr",   "value": "10.9.0.0/16", "provenance": "env" }
]

The provenance snapshot is frozen onto the run (variable_provenance) for audit, and the UI uses it to show "inherited from common-aws", "overridden here" or MOCK.

docs.title: Variable sets
docs.text:
Create a set, add members, then attach it. auto_attach: true attaches it to every stack in the space; otherwise attach explicitly to a tier, stack or environment, with a priority. A set is created in the default space unless you pass space_id.

SET=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/variable-sets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"common-aws","auto_attach":true}' | jq -r .id)

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/variable-sets/$SET/attachments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"target_kind":"environment","target_id":"'"$ENV"'","priority":10}'

docs.title: Attachments stay inside the set's space
docs.text:
A variable set only ever reaches its own space:

  • A stack or environment attachment requires the target to live in the set's space, and you need writer on it. Otherwise the attach is refused: 400 Cross-space attachment (or 403 when you can't write the target).
  • A tier attachment (target_id = the tier's id from GET /api/v1/tiers) applies to that tier's environments inside the set's space only. Tiers are a global catalog; attaching prod-credentials to the prod tier never injects it into another space's prod environments.
  • At resolution, an attachment from a set of another space is ignored, even one created before this rule existed.

Note

Detach a set before deleting it. Deleting an attached set returns 409 with the list of attachments — explicit detachment is required. Deleting a stack or an environment removes the attachments that target it for you (audited variable_set.detached with the reason).

docs.title: Sensitive values
docs.text:
Mark a variable sensitive: true to make it write-only:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/stacks/$STACK/variables \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"kind":"environment","name":"DD_API_KEY","value":"super-secret","sensitive":true}'

The value is AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest, decrypted only to build the worker claim payload, and the agent masks the literal value in logs.

Warning

A sensitive value is never returned in clear. A later GET shows "value": "•••"; the plaintext is not readable again through the API.

docs.title: Values by reference (external secret sources)
docs.text: Instead of storing a secret in Stackd, a variable can point at an entry in an external secrets manager (Proton Pass today). The value is fetched live at run time and never persisted — see External secret sources.

docs.title: Workers & scaling
docs.text:
Workers are the agents that actually run Terraform/OpenTofu. They are self-hosted, stateless and disposable: they pull work from the API and run each job in an ephemeral workspace. The API is the single source of truth; workers hold no durable state and can be killed and replaced at any time.

This page covers how the pull model works, how to run workers, and how to scale them.

docs.title: The pull model
docs.text:
A worker has no inbound ports. The API never connects out to it. Instead the worker drives everything:

  1. Register to a pool with the pool token → it gets a worker_id and a per-worker token. The token expires (default 24h); the worker re-registers automatically on a 401 to refresh it.
  2. Heartbeat every ~20s. The heartbeat response is the only downward channel (e.g. diagnostics, and later cancel_job).
  3. Claim a job via long-poll (POST /worker/v1/jobs/claim?wait=25), returning 204 when there is nothing to do.
  4. Run the job: clone the repo, run hooks + init/plan/apply (or the command), stream logs, report results and upload artifacts — including the saved plan the apply will use.
  5. Clean up the workspace and repeat.
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Worker
    participant A as API
    W->>A: POST /worker/v1/register (pool token)
    A-->>W: worker_id + worker_token
    loop every ~20s
        W->>A: POST /worker/v1/heartbeat
        A-->>W: { commands: [...] }
    end
    W->>A: POST /worker/v1/jobs/claim?wait=25
    A-->>W: 200 { job } | 204 nothing
    Note over W: clone → hooks → init → plan/apply → report

The queue is Postgres, not a broker. A claim is an atomic SELECT … FOR UPDATE … SKIP LOCKED that picks the next eligible run. There is no Redis, no RabbitMQ, nothing to operate beyond the database.

docs.title: One active run per environment
docs.text:
SKIP LOCKED alone does not serialise two workers claiming two distinct queued runs of the same environment. The hard guarantee is the partial unique index one_active_run_per_env: the second claim violates it (SQLSTATE 23505), is caught, and is treated as "nothing to claim" — that worker simply re-polls. The claim also locks the environment row (FOR UPDATE OF environment) so losers skip it and pick other work instead of wasting effort.

The practical consequence: the unit of parallelism is the environment. Two environments of the same stack run in parallel; two runs on the same environment never do.

docs.title: Apply affinity
docs.text: After a plan is confirmed, the originating worker is preferred for the apply for ~60s (STACKD_APPLY_AFFINITY_SECONDS). Past that delay (a dead or saturated worker), any compatible worker takes it. No workspace is reused either way: the apply worker clones the run's pinned commit, downloads the saved plan from the API and runs tofu apply plan.tfplan. It never re-plans: without a usable saved plan the run fails, and you trigger a new plan. See Runs & approvals.

docs.title: Worker loss
docs.text:
A worker silent for > 60s is marked offline. The scheduler (every 10 s) then fails the runs whose job is executing on that worker — preparing, planning, checking, running (a command) or applying — as failed (worker_lost), once the worker has been silent for > 120s. No human action required.

Runs that are not executing are never reclaimed: an unconfirmed run waits for a human and a confirmed one for the apply claim, and neither depends on the plan worker. Losing the worker that planned a run doesn't fail it; another worker applies the saved plan.

A job holding apply credentials — an applying run, or a mutating command run (import, state rm/mv, taint, untaint, refresh) — is the exception: it is reclaimed only after the apply window, the apply budget plus a grace period (stackd_apply_timeout_seconds + stackd_apply_lost_grace_seconds, default 15 min + 5 min). The worker hard-kills its own apply or mutating command at the budget, and that job's state token and apply OIDC token expire at the end of the window. So a healthy long apply is never failed mid-flight, and by the time the environment is handed to another run, the lost worker can no longer write its state. As a second safeguard, the state backend refuses a write or a lock from any token whose run has already ended.

docs.title: Time budgets
docs.text:
Each job's subprocesses run in their own process group: whatever a hook or a tofu command leaves running there is killed once it exits, and a watchdog kills the whole group past its budget. A plan, an apply or a command killed this way fails the run with an "exceeded the …s time budget" error:

What Budget apply of the saved plan the apply budget, apply_timeout_seconds in the claim (STACKD_APPLY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS on the API, default 900 s) a command run's subcommand the apply budget when the claim's cred_phase is apply (a mutating command); the default cap when it is plan (a read-only command). A missing or unknown cred_phase (an older API) gets the apply budget: it fails closed each hook the hook timeout, STACKD_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS on the worker (default 600 s). A hook past it fails by its own on_failure (Hooks) anything else (init, plan, show, output) the agent's default cap, 2 h

The worker never decides on its own whether a command is mutating: it reads cred_phase from the claim. A plan fails on any exit code but 0 (no changes) and 2 (changes) — a killed plan never passes for "no changes".

docs.title: Create a pool
docs.text:
Workers register to a pool, scoped to a space (space_id in the request, the default space otherwise). The pool token is shown once at creation and stored hashed. There is no rotate endpoint: if a token leaks, delete the pool and create a new one.

AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
POOL_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/worker-pools \
  -H "$AUTH" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "default"}' | jq -r .token)

docs.title: Run a worker
docs.text:
A worker needs only the API URL and the pool token (or STACKD_POOL_TOKEN_FILE, a file it re-reads until the token appears):

cd worker
STACKD_API_URL=http://localhost:8000 \
STACKD_POOL_TOKEN=$POOL_TOKEN \
  uv run python -m agent.main

docs.title: Worker settings
docs.text:
Variable Default What it does STACKD_API_URL http://api:8000 where the worker reaches the API STACKD_POOL_TOKEN / STACKD_POOL_TOKEN_FILE — the pool token, or a file holding it STACKD_WORKER_NAME the host name the worker's name in the UI STACKD_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS 1 jobs run at once, always on different environments STACKD_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 600 each hook's time budget STACKD_LEAK_TRIPWIRE warn fail fails a plan whose non-sensitive output shows a secret STACKD_WORKSPACE_ROOT /tmp/stackd-ws where each job's workspace is created, then removed STACKD_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL, STACKD_POLL_WAIT 20, 25 (s) heartbeat period, claim long-poll

These STACKD_* settings are the agent's own: they never reach tofu or a hook, so repo code can't read the pool token from its environment.

Keep platform secrets out of the worker's environment

The worker needs no database, S3 or signing credential: it reaches states and saved plans through the API. tofu and platform hooks inherit the worker's environment — minus the STACKD_* namespace — and repo code runs inside tofu (data "external", provisioners). So never give the worker DATABASE_URL, S3_* keys or GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, nor STACKD_ENCRYPTION_KEY or STACKD_JWT_SECRET. The dev compose file blanks them for the worker. Repo hooks get only an allowlist (PATH, HOME, locale, proxy and CA settings), see Hooks.

docs.title: Runners
docs.text:
Every job runs in its own workspace, removed when the job ends. Today the agent runs each tofu and hook command as a local subprocess, as its own OS user — whatever STACKD_RUNNER says. A container runner (STACKD_RUNNER=docker: each job in its own container from a runner image, see deploy/images/) is specified but not implemented yet. Until it exists, a job is isolated neither from the agent's own process nor from the other jobs of its worker: keep STACKD_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS=1 on workers that run code you don't fully trust.

Fargate caveat, for the container runner

A container runner needs to launch containers, i.e. Docker-in-Docker. AWS Fargate does not allow this. On Fargate, the worker runs commands locally, as it does today.

docs.title: Dedicate a pool with labels
docs.text:
Labels route work to pools. A run is eligible for a worker only when env.labels <@ worker.labels (the environment's labels are a subset of the worker's). To dedicate a pool to production, label both the prod environments and a prod-only worker pool with tier: prod, and give general workers no such label — they will never pick up prod runs.

# environment
labels: { tier: prod }
# prod worker pool / workers
labels: { tier: prod }

This is the recommended isolation for sensitive environments: combine it with prod-scoped cloud credentials for a hardened apply path.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
Scaling = run more workers. They are stateless, so just increase the replica count — e.g. an ECS service desiredCount, a Deployment replicas, or more agent processes. Nothing to coordinate; they all long-poll the same queue.

Because the environment is the unit of parallelism, throughput ≈ min(workers, environments with queued work). Adding workers beyond the number of environments that currently have queued runs buys nothing; they will idle on 204.

There is no built-in autoscaler, but the signals you need are exposed:

  • GET /api/v1/health — DB, workers (online/total + last heartbeat), runs active/queued, recent errors.
  • GET /api/v1/queue — waiting runs and why they wait (active_run | env_locked | no_compatible_worker | apply_affinity_hold).

A no_compatible_worker backlog means a label mismatch, not a capacity problem — adding generic workers will not help; you need workers carrying the right labels. See Observability for the Workers & health page.
